name: Nova Carter
desc: Nova Carter is NVIDIA's reference autonomous mobile robot for research and development on Isaac, integrating the Nova Orin sensor/compute architecture (multi-camera, LiDAR) for mapping, navigation and embodied-AI experimentation.

name: Stuntronics
desc: An autonomous, self-correcting aerial-performer robot — effectively a robotic stunt double — from Walt Disney Imagineering, built to make superhero characters fly in park attractions. Slung from a wire like a trapeze artist, the ~90 lb humanoid figure (three body sections joined by two flexible, pneumatically actuated joints) reads its own motion in mid-air with an onboard accelerometer/gyroscope IMU and three laser rangefinders, then tucks or untucks to control its rotation, pose and centre of mass — nailing flips, twists and even a quintuple somersault before sticking a targeted, feet-first landing in a heroic pose. It grew out of Imagineering's BRICK and Stickman research projects and has been used as a flying Spider-Man double at Avengers Campus.
actuator_type: Servo + onboard accelerometer/gyro
capabilities: Flips, twists, tucked landing, mid-air heroic poses (to quintuple somersault)

name: Vyloo
desc: A set of three small, autonomous animatronic alien creatures (the avian Vyloo from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2) from Walt Disney Imagineering's 'Automatronics' / Autonomous Characters research — among Disney's first park animatronics that actually respond to and interact with guests rather than looping a scripted show. Perched on a self-contained log/pod in the queue of Guardians of the Galaxy - Mission: BREAKOUT! at Disney California Adventure, each Vyloo has its own personality driven by decision-making algorithms (how long to hold eye contact, how fast to turn its head, whether to 'fall asleep'). Cameras and sensors let them track whether guests look at or talk to them and follow people with their gaze, conveying mood through simple 'squash-and-stretch' gestures, head cocks and kissy faces. Everything runs onboard, making them unusually modular. First shown ~2018 under the project name 'Tiny Life'.
actuator_type: Servo-driven (squash-and-stretch head/neck)
ai_model: Personality algorithms + animation blending + computer vision
behavior: Squash-and-stretch, head cocking, gaze-following, kissy faces
deployed_at: Guardians of the Galaxy - Mission: BREAKOUT! (Disney California Adventure)

name: RoboCoaster
desc: A passenger-carrying amusement ride built from a KUKA industrial robot arm — the concept was invented by Gino De-Gol (RoboCoaster Ltd, England) and realised with KUKA in 2001 from the adapted KR500 robot, debuting in 2002 with ten units sold to Legoland Denmark. A gondola of two to four seats is mounted to the wrist of a 6-axis arm, giving riders full six-degrees-of-freedom motion (360-degree pitch, yaw and roll well beyond a normal hexapod motion base) at up to ~2 g. Riders pick their own intensity from level 1 (gentle single-axis rotation) to level 5 (wild, inverted), and multiple stored motion profiles can be swapped at the press of a button. KUKA's certified passenger robots (KR 600 R2830 for up to 3 riders, KR 700 R2510 for up to 4) are TUV-certified to EN 13814 with redundant PLe brakes and optical encoders sampling arm position every 32 ms. Deployed in theme parks, VR motion simulators (RoboSim 4-D) and dark rides worldwide, including Epcot's 'Sum of All Thrills'.
actuator_type: 6-axis industrial robot (KR-series servo)

name: Kime
desc: A humanoid robotic bartender/barista from Spain's Macco Robotics (Seville). Kime stands about two meters tall with dual articulating arms that pour a beer in under 8 seconds and mix a cocktail in around 30 — up to ~120 drinks an hour across beers, cocktails, juices and soft drinks. It engages customers by touchscreen (and mobile-app ordering) in their preferred language, takes cashless payments, and wears an antimicrobial, food-grade shell with automated cleaning routines. Built for 'plug-and-play' integration with existing bar equipment and offered with swappable beverage modules and custom branding, it's aimed at bars, restaurants, events and promotional activations. The current v5 was demonstrated in Seville hospitality trials in 2026.

name: Cecilia
desc: Billed as the world's first interactive robotic bartender, Cecilia.ai (from Israel's GKI hospitality-tech group) is an arcade-console-sized kiosk about seven feet tall, fronted by a large touchscreen showing a 3D-animated female bartender who chats, tells jokes, recommends drinks and displays promos when idle. Guests order by voice (contactless) or touchscreen; conversational AI with voice recognition — scripted plus machine learning — keeps the banter going, in up to 40 languages. Behind the screen, an articulating arm dispenses precisely measured pours from 12 ingredient containers (~70 L total) to make up to 120 cocktails an hour, delivered through a slot. It can't garnish or make ice, but adds brandable side LEDs (disco mode included), cashless payment, and a business-intelligence dashboard of popular drinks and peak times. Seen at stadiums, airport and VIP lounges, cruises and events.

name: EX Robots Humanoid Android
desc: A series of hyper-realistic humanoid androids from China's EX Robots (Dalian Tiasi Technology Development Co.), known for their lifelike human appearance. A mechanical metal body is wrapped in 3D-printed silicone skin over the face, hands and feet, and micro-motor actuators drive both the flexible joints and the facial 'muscles' to reproduce nuanced expressions, eye contact and gestures. Patented joint designs give an extensive range of motion. Control is via preset behaviour programs, smartphone/tablet apps and guided modes, with onboard cameras and microphones for perception and voice interaction. EX Robots is pioneering mass-production of customisable androids for service, entertainment, rescue and science-education roles.
actuator_type: Micro-motor + proprietary flexible joints
manufacturer_history: EX Robot / EX Robots (Dalian Tiasi Technology Development Co.), Dalian, Liaoning, China. Founded 2013 (R&D from 2009) by Li Boyang (PhD AI, Waseda 2010). Ultra-realistic bionic androids. 150+ patents. Opened EX Future Science & Technology Museum (Dalian, 2021) — China's first robot museum, 30+ robots.

name: GoBe
desc: GoBe (Blue Ocean Robotics) is an enterprise telepresence robot with autonomous navigation, HD video and a tall display, marketed around cutting business travel and CO2 - each unit can offset several tons of travel emissions per user annually. Used in offices, factories and healthcare.
use_cases: Telepresence for offices, healthcare & education (autonomous navigation + mapping)

name: OhmniCare
desc: OhmniCare (OhmniLabs, now part of Symbotic) is a healthcare-focused telepresence robot that replaced the original Ohmni in 2024, with a fully emotive neck, 4K video and one-click connection, designed for remote clinical rounds, tele-nursing and patient consults.
use_cases: Healthcare telepresence — remote patient visits & senior care

name: A2
desc: The AMY Robotics A2 is an autonomous-navigation telepresence robot with an adjustable-height display, HD camera and obstacle avoidance, used for remote office presence, healthcare rounds and remote inspection.
use_cases: Healthcare & office telepresence with autonomous navigation

name: PadBot P3
desc: The PadBot P3 (Inbot Technology) is a mid-size telepresence robot with a built-in HD display and camera (no tablet required), remote-driveable via app for home, office and education remote-presence use.

name: Ballie
desc: Ballie is Samsung's bright-yellow rolling home AI companion, powered by Google Gemini and Samsung's own models. It holds natural conversations, controls smart-home devices, greets visitors, projects content via a built-in projector, and checks on pets/family with front 4K and rear 2K cameras. Launch slated for 2026.

name: Q9 (CLOi AI Agent)
desc: LG's 'Self-Driving AI Home Hub' — a cute companion robot that rolls around the house on two gyroscopic one-wheeled legs, balancing itself while it moves. With bright expressive eyes, cameras, a microphone array and generative-AI voice conversation, Q9 acts as a mobile personal assistant and the physical face of LG's ThinQ smart home: it greets and chats with the family, reports on overnight energy use, sleep and temperature, delivers weather and reminders, and relays commands to LG appliances. LG frames it around 'Affectionate Intelligence' — AI meant to understand and empathize with users — and offers it on a subscription model. It's the forerunner to LG's CLOiD home humanoid (CES 2026).
actuator_type: Two-wheeled self-balancing drive

name: Ropet
desc: A furry, big-eyed AI companion pet from Mengyou Intelligence — the first product from a company founded by He Jiabin, former head of ByteDance's PICO Beijing ID design team — launched via Kickstarter in late 2024 and shown at CES 2025. Ropet loves being stroked and reacts to voice, touch and gestures with cute animated-eye expressions and sounds. Cameras, microphones and sensors give it facial recognition (it knows its owner and reacts to your expressions), a 'mood radar', and the ability to recognise foods and objects held up to its face (dangle a toy hotdog and hotdogs flash across its eyes). name: Mirumi

Mirumi clips onto a bag handle or strap and does exactly one thing charmingly: it turns its single rotating head to 'peek' at nearby people. Using an internal IMU and a distance sensor, it scans its surroundings and, once it notices someone, fixes them with an innocent baby-like gaze — then acts bashful and hides its face, or gives a little bow when petted. Inspired by the warm feeling of catching a cute baby's eye in public, it has no voice or app; its whole purpose is to spark small moments of shared joy with strangers on a train or in a queue.

A microphone array lets it understand simple commands (tell it to 'speak' and it barks). Deliberately screen-free and low-tech, it's aimed at comfort for people with dementia, anxiety or sensory-processing needs; Tombot returned to CES 2026 positioning Jennie as an FDA-regulated robotic pet for clinical and long-term-care use, with 7,500+ preorders.

Co-designed with Jim Henson's Creature Shop for lifelike fur + movement, she's fully autonomous, responds to touch (body-wide capacitive sensors), voice (barks on command) + movement with authentic puppy behaviors (tail wags, head tilts, a 'heartbeat', real-puppy sound recordings). Deliberately lap-based (no floor roaming - trip-safety), all-day battery, app-customizable. Shown at CES 2025/2026; ~18,000+ preorders; Tombot is pursuing FDA medical-device recognition.

name: ARA
desc: The Ecorobotix ARA is an ultra-high-precision smart sprayer with six cameras and 156 nozzles achieving ~6x6 cm spray resolution, applying plant-by-plant microdoses and cutting chemical use by 70-95%. Tractor-towed, with 20+ crop-specific AI algorithms.
use_cases: AI plant-by-plant precision spraying (6 m boom, ~6x6 cm targeting)

name: FD20
desc: The FarmDroid FD20 is a fully solar-powered autonomous robot that both seeds and mechanically weeds row crops. It records each seed's RTK-GPS position (8 mm) at sowing, so it can weed between and within rows before plants even emerge. ~1,250 kg (low soil compaction), 18-24 h/day CO2-neutral operation, ~6 ha/day, 50+ crop types; the +Spray option cuts chemicals up to 94%.

name: E-Series
desc: The Agrobot E-Series is an AI-vision strawberry-harvesting robot with up to 24 independent robotic arms that identify ripe berries and pick them with ~1 cm tolerance, avoiding unripe fruit and minimising bruising for premium markets.
actuator_type: Up to 24 independent picking arms with AI ripeness vision

name: Astronaut A5
desc: The Lely Astronaut A5 is an automatic (robotic) milking system that lets cows be milked voluntarily on demand; a robotic arm with 3D laser-guided teat detection attaches the cups while the system tracks per-cow yield and health data.
actuator_type: Hybrid milking arm (electric + pneumatic)

name: Origin
desc: The Cruise Origin (GM) was a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free shared robotaxi. Development was wound down after GM ended Cruise's robotaxi program in 2024 - included here as a notable discontinued milestone in the robotaxi category.
use_cases: Shared autonomous ride-hailing (program wound down 2024; design never mass-deployed)

name: Gen-7 Robotaxi
desc: Pony.ai's seventh-generation Robotaxi entered mass production in 2025 - the first to use 100% automotive-grade components with a ~70% lower autonomous-driving-kit BOM. Pony.ai runs fully-driverless service across China's four tier-one cities.
config: Built on GAC & BAIC platforms; automotive-grade
feature: ~70% lower autonomous-kit BOM vs prior gen
cameras: Multi-sensor kit: LiDAR + radar + cameras (100% automotive-grade)
use_cases: Driverless robotaxi (Toyota, GAC & BAIC vehicle platforms, mass production 2025)

name: Autonomous Shuttle (Sienna)
desc: May Mobility operates autonomous microtransit shuttles (Toyota Sienna platform) for on-demand and fixed-route public transit in several US cities, moving toward driver-out L4 operation in defined service zones.
use_cases: Public microtransit shuttle service (multi-passenger autonomous transit)

name: Aurora Driver (Autonomous Truck)
desc: The Aurora Driver is a self-driving system for Class 8 freight trucks; Aurora launched commercial driverless freight runs on Texas highways (Dallas-Houston) in 2025, hauling loads with no human in the cab.
use_cases: Driverless freight (Aurora Horizon subscription; launched commercial driverless 2025)

name: Kodiak Driver
desc: The Kodiak Driver is a self-driving system for long-haul and off-road trucking; Kodiak delivered driverless commercial trucks for customers (including Permian Basin oilfield routes) and focuses on autonomous freight at scale.
use_cases: Driverless freight hauling (vehicle-agnostic, 2.5M+ test miles; Bosch manufacturing partnership)

name: Mission Master SP
desc: Low-profile 8x8 all-electric autonomous UGV (Silent Partner) built for forward and last-mile resupply, silent watch and carriage of section sensors or weapon systems. Weighs 1,134 kg, carries up to 1,000 kg (300 kg amphibious) and reaches 40 km/h, using Rheinmetall's PATH autonomy kit for follow-me, teleoperation and supervised autonomy. Networked with Rheinmetall's soldier system and C2 software; selected for trials by Japan's JGSDF and several NATO armies.
actuator_type: Electric 8x8 drivetrain (silent watch capable)

name: Titan
desc: A fully modular hybrid unmanned ground vehicle jointly developed by QinetiQ North America and Estonia's Milrem Robotics, built to 'lighten the load' for dismounted troops. Titan pairs Milrem's THeMIS (Tracked Hybrid Modular Infantry System) mobility base - two tracked drive modules linked by a mission payload frame - with QinetiQ's Tactical Robot Controller (a pocket 6.5-inch controller) and Robotic Applique Kit for autonomy, night-vision/thermal cameras and comms, operable in manned or unmanned modes at line-of-sight ranges over 800 m. It measures about 2.0 x 2.1 x 1.0 m with a curb weight near 907 kg and carries up to ~680 kg (with a 2,000 lb pull force). Its diesel-electric hybrid drive gives ~100 km range / up to 72 h endurance, or a run-silent all-electric mode good for 20+ km over ~2 hours. Its open architecture accepts modules for logistics/resupply, CASEVAC litters, earth-moving, route clearance, CBRN/RSTA and remote weapon stations. It contended in the US Army SMET and UK Dstl Last-Mile Resupply programs.
actuator_type: Modular tracked UGV (THeMIS-based)
propulsion: Diesel-electric hybrid (10 kW JP8 generator + AGM/Li-ion)
control: QinetiQ TRC + RAK; manned or unmanned
program: US Army SMET; UK Dstl Last-Mile Resupply

name: Optio-X20
desc: The KNDS/Nexter Optio-X20 is a tracked robotic combat platform (and the Ultro-600 robotic mule sibling) evaluated by European armies for logistics and armed support roles, carrying up to ~600 kg.
use_cases: Remote weapon platform, ISR, cargo (20-tonne class tracked UGV)

name: Ripsaw M5
desc: Fifth-generation Ripsaw — a tracked Robotic Combat Vehicle developed by Team Ripsaw (Textron Systems, Howe & Howe and Teledyne FLIR) for the US Army's RCV-Medium effort. Hybrid diesel-electric drivetrain, flat open architecture and configurable armour, with a 10.5-tonne combat weight, ~3,600 kg payload and 65 km/h top speed. Can mount a Kongsberg MCT-30 turret (30/40 mm Bushmaster), carry the R80D SkyRaider UAS and uses the SUMIT 360° EO/IR perception suite.
actuator_type: Hybrid diesel-electric drivetrain, tracked
use_cases: Robotic combat vehicle (US Army RCV-M candidate)
made_in: USA (Textron Systems / Howe & Howe — Team Lynx)

name: Gereon RCS
desc: The ARX Robotics Gereon RCS is a lightweight tracked UGV for European armed forces, used for logistics, reconnaissance and as a mobile sensor/effector carrier; designed for scalable, software-defined autonomy.
use_cases: Logistics, casualty evacuation, ISR (scalable modular platform)

name: TRX (Tracked Robot 10-ton)
desc: General Dynamics Land Systems' medium-class tracked unmanned ground vehicle, unveiled at AUSA 2021 and entered as GDLS's contender in the US Army's Robotic Combat Vehicle (RCV) program. As its name suggests, the TRX is designed around a 10-ton class: roughly a 5-ton curb weight plus up to a 5-ton payload on a flat modular deck. Because there's no crew to armour, it uses lightweight materials and a hybrid-electric drive that lowers its thermal signature, enables near-silent running and powers onboard electronics, while keeping pace with fast Armoured Brigade Combat Teams. Its open, payload-agnostic architecture lets the Army swap mission modules quickly, and it's built for manned-unmanned teaming as a 'wingman' to crewed vehicles. Derived from GDLS's MUTT program, published mission roles include tactical resupply, counter-UAS/short-range air defence, obstacle breaching, indirect fire, electronic warfare and ISR; a SHORAD variant can autonomously launch and recover small UAS.
actuator_type: Hybrid-electric tracked drivetrain
uas: Autonomous launch/recovery of small UAS (SHORAD variant)

name: PROBOT
desc: Compact wheeled logistics UGV able to carry around 750 kg of supplies or evacuate casualties while following a squad autonomously or under teleoperation. Built with an open architecture for mission modules including ISR masts, RWS and CBRN sensors, and integrated with Roboteam's control suite shared across its robot family.

name: Skypod
desc: The Exotec Skypod is a goods-to-person warehouse robot that drives on the floor and climbs storage racks up to ~12 m to retrieve bins, combining high-density storage with fast picking. Travels ~4 m/s; deployed by major retailers and 3PLs worldwide.
use_cases: Goods-to-person warehouse fulfillment (climbs racks to 12 m)

name: HaiPick A42
desc: The Hai Robotics HaiPick A42 is an autonomous case-handling robot that retrieves multiple totes/cartons from high racks (up to ~10 m) and delivers them to pick stations, pioneering the ACR category for dense, flexible warehouse storage.
actuator_type: Telescopic-mast autonomous case-handling robot (multi-tote)

name: Ranger
desc: The GreyOrange Ranger family are goods-to-person and sortation AMRs that move racks or totes to operators, orchestrated by GreyOrange's GreyMatter fulfilment software for retail and e-commerce warehouses.
use_cases: Warehouse goods-to-person & sortation AMR fleet (GreyMatter software)

name: Palion Tow Tractor
desc: The Seegrid Palion Tow Tractor is a vision-guided (camera-based, infrastructure-free) autonomous tow tractor for material movement in manufacturing and warehousing, part of Seegrid's Palion line alongside pallet trucks and lift trucks.

name: Vecna RPL (Robotic Pallet Lift)
desc: Vecna Robotics builds autonomous pallet trucks and tuggers for warehouse material handling, with the Pivotal orchestration platform and a human-in-the-loop remote support model for handling edge cases.

name: MiR1200 Pallet Jack
desc: The MiR1200 Pallet Jack (Mobile Industrial Robots, a Teradyne company) uses AI-powered 3D vision to autonomously locate, pick and deliver pallets, carrying up to ~1,200 kg - extending the MiR AMR line into pallet handling.

name: Pegasus
desc: Amazon Robotics Pegasus is a compact drive unit with a conveyor top that carries individual packages across a sortation floor and tips them into the correct chute, improving package-sorting accuracy in Amazon fulfilment centres.
actuator_type: Drive unit with conveyor top module
use_cases: Package sortation in Amazon fulfillment centers

name: FoxBot
desc: The Fox Robotics FoxBot is an autonomous trailer-unloading forklift that automatically unloads palletised freight from trucks at the dock, addressing one of the most labour-intensive and injury-prone warehouse tasks.
use_cases: Autonomous trailer unloading & dock work (robotic forklift)

name: inVia Picker
desc: The inVia Picker is a goods-to-person robot that autonomously retrieves totes from standard shelving and brings them to pick stations, offered under a robotics-as-a-service model for e-commerce fulfilment.

name: da Vinci 5
desc: The Intuitive da Vinci 5 (FDA-cleared March 2024) is the fifth-generation multiport robotic-assisted surgery system, adding first-of-its-kind Force Feedback, a new 3D display and 150+ enhancements over da Vinci Xi. Used across most surgical specialties; going international through 2025.
key_feature: Force Feedback technology; ~10,000x compute of da Vinci Xi
actuator_type: Force-feedback instrument arms (first in da Vinci line)

name: Ottava
desc: Ottava is Johnson & Johnson MedTech's soft-tissue surgical robot, uniquely integrating four arms into the operating table for a low profile and flexible setup. First US clinical cases (incl. gastric bypass) were completed in 2025, with an FDA submission expected in early 2026.
approach: Four arms integrated into the OR table
regulatory: Investigational - first US clinical cases done; FDA submission expected early 2026
use_cases: Multi-specialty soft-tissue surgery (6 arms integrated into the OR table; clinical trials underway)

name: Maestro
desc: The Moon Surgical Maestro is an accessible surgical-assistance robot that works with standard laparoscopic instruments, adding two robotic arms to hold and position the camera and tools - designed to fit existing OR workflows affordably. FDA-cleared and CE-marked.
key_feature: Two assistive arms that fit existing OR workflow
use_cases: Collaborative laparoscopic surgery (works with existing instruments; FDA-cleared & CE-marked)

name: Mazor X Stealth
desc: The Medtronic Mazor X Stealth Edition is a spine surgical robot combining preoperative planning with robotic guidance and integrated navigation for precise pedicle-screw and implant placement.
use_cases: Robotic-guided spine surgery with StealthStation navigation & predictive analytics

name: Senhance
desc: The Asensus Senhance is a digital laparoscopic surgical system with reusable instruments, haptic force feedback and eye-tracking camera control, aiming to lower per-procedure cost while adding digital intelligence to surgery.
key_feature: Haptic force feedback + eye-tracking camera control
actuator_type: Laparoscopic arms with haptic feedback
use_cases: Digital laparoscopic surgery with reusable instruments

name: CORI
desc: The Smith+Nephew CORI Surgical System is a compact handheld robotic platform for partial and total knee replacement, using real-time bone mapping (no preoperative CT) and a robotics-assisted bur for precise resurfacing.
actuator_type: Handheld robotic milling (real-time bone cutting)

name: CyberKnife S7
desc: The Accuray CyberKnife S7 mounts a linear accelerator on a robotic arm to deliver highly targeted radiation to tumours from many angles, with real-time motion tracking that adjusts for patient and tumour movement.
actuator_type: Robotic manipulator with linear accelerator, real-time motion tracking (Synchrony)

name: Monarch Platform
desc: The Monarch Platform (J&J MedTech, originally Auris Health) is a robotic flexible-endoscopy system using a controller-driven scope for peripheral lung biopsy (bronchoscopy) and kidney-stone removal (urology), with navigation guidance.
actuator_type: Flexible robotic endoscope platform

name: PUDU T300
desc: The PUDU T300 is an industrial-grade autonomous delivery robot for factories and warehouses, carrying heavy loads with high precision and integrating with lifts and automatic doors for end-to-end material flow.

name: PUDU CC1 Pro
desc: The AI-powered edition of Pudu Robotics' flagship commercial floor cleaner — a 4-in-1 robot that sweeps, scrubs, vacuums and dust-mops in a single pass. The Pro adds proactive intelligence: it automatically detects stains and surface changes, adjusts cleaning intensity on the fly, and self-monitors to prevent secondary contamination. Its VSLAM+ and LiDAR fusion navigation maps and cleans complex spaces with no floor QR codes or markers, and it runs up to 8 hours per charge (3-hour recharge) at speeds up to ~1.2 m/s. With 15 L clean and 15 L dirty water tanks (auto fill/empty), autonomous docking and auto dust-tank disposal, and auto-resume after low battery, it's built for hands-off operation in hotels, multifamily housing, schools, offices, gyms and assisted-living facilities. About 629 x 552 x 695 mm and ~75 kg; listed around $24,000 with RaaS/lease options.
navigation: VSLAM+ & LiDAR fusion (PUDU SLAM, no QR codes)

name: HolaBot
desc: The Pudu HolaBot is a heavy-load (~60 kg) delivery and bussing robot with large enclosed shelves, used for food running and dish return in busy restaurants; summoned via call bells and capable of dish-collection cycles.

name: KLEENBOT C30
desc: The KEENON KLEENBOT C30 is a commercial floor-cleaning robot combining sweeping, scrubbing and drying with autonomous navigation for malls, airports and offices.
use_cases: Commercial floor cleaning (sweep, vacuum, dust mop — 61 cm width, 19,000 Pa suction, 2,500 m² per charge)

name: Whiz
desc: The SoftBank Whiz is an autonomous commercial vacuum-sweeping robot (BrainOS-powered) for offices, hotels and retail, learning routes by being driven once then repeating them autonomously; SoftBank's flagship after refocusing from the Pepper humanoid.
use_cases: Commercial vacuum cleaning (up to 1,500 m² per charge)
manufacturer_history: SoftBank Robotics (Japan/France). Pepper unveiled 2014 by Masayoshi Son (built with French Aldebaran, maker of NAO) — world's first full-scale humanoid offered to consumers (2015, ¥198,000). NAOqi OS. In 2022 United Robotics Group acquired SoftBank Robotics Europe, reverting to Aldebaran name.

name: Neo
desc: The flagship of Avidbots (Kitchener, Ontario) and one of the most widely deployed autonomous floor-scrubbing robots — used across airports, warehouses (DHL, DSV) and malls, where it reportedly removes up to 80% of manual cleaning labour hours. Powered by Avidbots Autonomy, Neo maps and cleans a site on its own with dynamic path planning, real-time obstacle avoidance and 360-degree visibility from a market-leading sensor suite, no operator required. It offers a 24 in or 32 in cleaning path with disc or cylindrical heads, a ~132 L (35 gal) solution tank, coverage up to ~3,900 m2/hr, and up to six hours of run time per AGM battery — extendable by simply swapping batteries. It accepts standard low-foaming floor detergents.

name: T7AMR
desc: Tennant Company's autonomous ride-on robotic floor scrubber, built on its T7 micro-rider and made self-driving by Brain Corp's vision-based BrainOS platform (learn-and-repeat routes with real-world obstacle avoidance). It cleans a 650 mm (26 in) path with two 0.45 kW brush motors at 225 rpm and up to 86 kg of down-pressure to lift embedded grime, fed by equal 110 L solution and recovery tanks for theoretical productivity up to 4,250 m2/hr. The 24 V machine runs ~4 hours on lead-acid (up to 6.5 hours on lithium-ion, or a 9.2 kWh Li-Ion pack), cleans as quietly as 70 dBA for daytime use, and uses ec-H2O NanoClean to cut water and detergent. It measures 1650 x 850 x 1450 mm, weighs ~492 kg, and reports fleet KPIs weekly.

name: K5
desc: The Knightscope K5 is a large autonomous outdoor security robot that patrols parking lots, campuses and malls, streaming 360° video, reading licence plates and detecting anomalies, offered on a Robot-as-a-Service subscription.

name: CLOi ServeBot
desc: LG's autonomous serving and delivery robot (model LDLIM21), launched in the US in early 2022 and named one of Time's Best Inventions of 2022 — notable as the world's first commercial service robot to earn UL 3300 safety certification for open, dynamic environments. Standing 1,339 mm tall on a compact 510 x 510 mm footprint, it carries up to 30 kg across three open shelves (10 kg each) and moves at up to 1 m/s, running as long as 11 hours on its 23,000 mAh battery (0-100% in 5 hours). It fuses LiDAR, a 3D camera, ToF and bumper sensors for obstacle avoidance, with a ToF sensor on each shelf so it knows when an item is taken and moves to the next stop. A 9.2-inch touchscreen shows cartoon eye animations and handles setup, voice and music, and cloud connectivity enables remote monitoring and free OTA updates. Used in restaurants, hotels, retail and healthcare.

name: Gen3 Delivery Robot
desc: The Serve Robotics third-generation sidewalk delivery robot (spun out of Uber) runs Level 4 autonomy on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin brain with Ouster LiDAR, ~11 mph top speed, ~14 h battery and ~15 gal insulated cargo (holds 4x 16" pizzas). Serve deployed its 2,000th robot in 2025 across LA, Miami, Dallas, Chicago and Atlanta with Uber Eats and DoorDash.

name: Coco Bot
desc: Coco operates pink insulated sidewalk delivery robots for restaurant orders, using a remote-piloted-plus-autonomy model for safe urban navigation; widely deployed in Los Angeles and other US cities.

name: Delivery Robot
desc: Avride (spun out of Yandex's self-driving group) builds six-wheeled autonomous sidewalk delivery robots deployed with Uber Eats and Grubhub, alongside its autonomous-vehicle work; operates in several US cities.

name: Ottobot Yeti
desc: The Ottonomy Ottobot is a fully-autonomous delivery robot used both indoors (airports, retail) and outdoors (curbside, sidewalk), with contextual-AI navigation and multi-compartment cargo for parcels, food and pharmacy.
actuator_type: 4-wheel independent steering (crab mode)

name: Neolix Delivery Vehicle
desc: Neolix builds compact driverless delivery vans for last-mile logistics, retail-on-wheels and contactless delivery, deployed at scale across Chinese cities for parcel and grocery distribution.
use_cases: Level-4 urban unmanned delivery vehicle (retail, logistics, vending)

name: Ingenuity
desc: Ingenuity was NASA/JPL's Mars helicopter - the first powered, controlled flight on another planet (Apr 2021). Just 1.8 kg with counter-rotating rotors and solar charging, it flew 72 times over ~3 years (vs a 5-flight plan), covering ~17 km, before rotor-blade damage grounded it in Jan 2024.
achievement: First powered, controlled flight on another planet
actuator_type: 2x coaxial counter-rotating rotors

name: Nova-C (Odysseus)
desc: The Intuitive Machines Nova-C "Odysseus" was the first US lunar lander since Apollo and the first commercial soft landing on the Moon (IM-1, Feb 2024). A ~1,900 kg hexagonal-cylinder lander (100 kg payload) that touched down near the lunar south pole, tipping on landing but returning data.
achievement: First US lunar landing since Apollo; first commercial soft landing
payload_instruments: SCALPSS, ROLSES, NDL LIDAR, ILO-X, LN-1

name: Astrobee
desc: Astrobee is NASA's system of cube-shaped free-flying robots (Bumble, Honey, Queen) aboard the ISS, using electric impeller fans to fly weightlessly and cameras/sensors to navigate the Kibo module - assisting astronauts and hosting student programming challenges.
actuator_type: Electric impeller fan propulsion

name: SORA-Q (LEV-2)
desc: SORA-Q (LEV-2) is JAXA's baseball-sized (~250 g) transformable lunar rover deployed by the SLIM "Moon Sniper" lander (Jan 2024). It splits open into a two-wheeled crawler to image the lander and terrain - co-developed with toy maker Tomy, Sony and Doshisha University.
actuator_type: Transformable split-shell crawling drive

name: CADRE Rovers
desc: CADRE (Cooperative Autonomous Distributed Robotic Explorers) is a set of small shoebox-sized NASA rovers designed to operate together autonomously as a team on the Moon, demonstrating multi-robot coordination; manifested on the IM-3 mission.
objective: Autonomous multi-robot coordination on the Moon
use_cases: Cooperative multi-robot lunar exploration (3 autonomous shoebox-sized rovers mapping in formation; Intuitive Machines IM-3 delivery)
actuator_type: 4-wheel rover, solar powered

name: CIMON
desc: CIMON (Crew Interactive Mobile Companion) is a free-floating, AI-powered spherical assistant aboard the ISS, built by Airbus for DLR with IBM Watson voice AI - it talks with astronauts, displays procedures and floats via internal fans.
actuator_type: 12 internal fans (free-flying in microgravity)
cameras: Front camera + microphones for crew interaction

name: Canadarm3
desc: Canadarm3 is Canada's AI-enabled robotic system for NASA's Lunar Gateway - a smart, largely autonomous arm (built by MDA) that will maintain, repair and inspect the Gateway station in lunar orbit without constant human control.

name: European Robotic Arm (ERA)
desc: The European Robotic Arm (ERA) is a ~11 m symmetrical robotic arm on the ISS Russian segment that can "walk" end-over-end between fixed base points to move payloads and assist spacewalks; built by Airbus for ESA.
actuator_type: Walks end-over-end between base points

name: VEX IQ
desc: A tool-less, snap-together robotics platform from VEX Robotics for grades 4–8, widely used in classrooms and the VEX IQ Robotics Competition. At its core is the IQ Robot Brain with a colour screen and twelve Smart Ports that auto-detect and interchangeably drive Smart Motors (each with a built-in processor, quadrature encoder and current monitor) and sensors — Optical (colour/light/gesture), laser Distance, Touch LED and Bumper — with a 6-axis gyro/accelerometer built into the 2nd-gen Brain. A game-controller-style handheld drives it wirelessly over VEXnet/Bluetooth. Students program in VEXcode IQ using Blocks, Python or C++ across browser, Windows, Mac and ChromeOS, with automatic firmware updates via VEXos.

name: VEX GO
desc: An affordable snap-together STEM construction system from VEX Robotics aimed at ages 7–11, designed so young students can tinker, make mistakes and try again. The education kit packs 296 structural and motion components with a GO Robot Brain, three motors, three electromagnets, an eye (optical) sensor, an LED bumper switch, a rechargeable battery and storage cases. Kids code it with block-based VEXcode GO (Scratch-style) right in the browser at codeGO.vex.com — no installation — on tablets, Chromebooks, Macs or PCs, supported by VEX STEM Labs cross-curriculum lesson plans spanning language arts, math, coding and engineering.
curriculum: VEX STEM Labs (language arts, math, coding, engineering)

name: mBot2
desc: The Makeblock mBot2 is an upgraded entry-level coding robot built on the CyberPi controller with Wi-Fi, supporting Scratch and Python; popular as a school class-pack for line-following, obstacle avoidance and AIoT projects.

name: mBot Ranger
desc: The Makeblock mBot Ranger is a 3-in-1 transformable robotics kit (tank, self-balancing car, three-wheel racer) with block-based mBlock and Arduino programming for intermediate STEM learners.
use_cases: 3-in-1 STEM build: tank / three-wheel racer / self-balancing robot

name: Cue
desc: An award-winning coding robot from Wonder Workshop (makers of Dash & Dot), built to carry students from block-based code into state-machine and text-based programming. Aimed at ages 11+, Cue ('Coding Utility Engine') has four selectable 'hero' avatar personalities with enhanced conversational AI and witty text-message-style chat. The wheeled robot moves expressively with RGB LED lights and a speaker, sensing its surroundings with IR proximity/distance sensors, microphones and an accelerometer, and connects over Bluetooth LE to the Wonder and Cue apps. Students program it in the block-based Wonder language and in JavaScript/Blockly. No longer produced, but still supported by Wonder Workshop.

name: JIMU Robot
desc: UBTECH JIMU Robot is a buildable STEM robotics kit line for children/education — snap-together servos, sensors and an app for coding, letting users build various robot forms. A consumer education product, not a humanoid.
actuator_type: Smart servo motors (snap-together kits)
manufacturer_history: UBTECH Robotics (Shenzhen, China), founded 2012. First Chinese humanoid company publicly listed (HKEX 2023). Consumer robots (Alpha, JIMU, Cruzr) → Walker humanoid series (Walker 1 2018 → Walker X 2021 → Walker S/S1/S2 industrial 2024-25). Walker S2 (Nov 2025) is world-first autonomous battery-swapping humanoid, in mass production (~$112M orders), deployed at BYD, Geely, FAW-VW, Audi, Foxconn, SF Express, Airbus.

raw_specs.note: App-coded modular kit, not a fixed humanoid

name: ROSMASTER X3
desc: The Yahboom ROSMASTER X3 is an advanced education robot supporting ROS2, SLAM, LiDAR and machine-learning modules on a mecanum-wheel base - a testbed bridging classroom STEM and real robotics research/Jetson development.
cpu: NVIDIA Jetson Nano / Orin NX options
actuator_type: Mecanum omnidirectional wheels

name: T1
desc: Booster Robotics' compact open-source developer humanoid and the model that won the 2025 RoboCup 'AdultSize' soccer league, adopted by 50+ teams and labs (Purdue, UC Berkeley, CMU, Tsinghua). Standing about 1.2 m and weighing 30 kg, it has 23 base DOF (6 per leg, 4 per arm, 1 waist, 2 head) driven by custom hollow-axis motors with dual encoders and full-force (torque/velocity/position) control up to 130 N·m. Dual compute — a 14-core Intel i7-1370P plus NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB (~200 TOPS) — runs onboard AI, with an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera, 3D LiDAR, 9-axis IMU and mic array. Fully open SDK on ROS2 with Isaac Sim / MuJoCo / Webots support and up to ~2 h walking per charge.
actuator_type: Full torque-controlled dual-encoder joint modules (hybrid torque/speed/position control)
cpu: Intel i7-1370P (14-core) + NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 32GB
chipset: Intel i7-1370P + NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 32GB
manufacturer_history: Booster Robotics (Beijing, founded 2023), 'Made for Developers'. T1 is a mid-size research/competition humanoid; used by the 2025 RoboCup AdultSize champions (Tsinghua 'Hephaestus'), Purdue, CMU (FALCON RL), and UC Berkeley (FastTD3). Line includes K1 (compact ~95 cm education platform) and T2.

raw_specs.Source: Booster docs (docs.bipedal.de) + robozaps / robotshop / aparobot / robotsasia / robotsinternational

name: CL-1
desc: The LimX Dynamics CL-1, debuted late 2023 by the Shenzhen startup (founded 2022), is one of the few humanoids capable of dynamic stair climbing via real-time terrain perception — the capability behind its viral warehouse-stairs video. At 1,650 mm, it was developed from LimX's point-foot biped P1 as a locomotion research platform, using proprietary hollow direct-drive actuators for deep squats, slope walking and push-recovery, with vision-LiDAR terrain perception at up to 4 km/h. Per LimX and The Robot Report, CL-1 was purely a bipedal platform and was never fitted with functional/articulated hands — later warehouse demos used simple paddle end-effectors to move totes. Hand-specific spec sections are therefore not applicable and omitted. Richer figures (31 DOF, 7-DOF arms, AGX Orin) belong to the later CL-3/Oli, not CL-1, and are excluded. Applicable-but-unpublished CL-1 fields are flagged 'Info not found' for outreach.

name: DR01
desc: The DEEP Robotics DR01 (Dr.01) is a full-size bipedal humanoid from Hangzhou's DEEP Robotics — the quadruped specialist (Lynx, X30) that entered the humanoid race positioning DR01 as an 'embodied intelligence explorer,' a platform to accelerate AI and big-data training for embodied intelligence. It walks at over 1.6 m/s and navigates 18 cm steps, 25° slopes and uneven, discrete terrain, swiftly recovering balance under unknown disturbances like slippery surfaces and external forces — demonstrations include stair climbing, walking across steel bars, and staying upright while pushed or pulled. It's built on DEEP Robotics' self-developed J60 lightweight joints and J100 high-torque joints, and its 'Fusion Perception' integrates self-perception with environmental perception through a learning algorithm that couples sensing and control, rather than relying on scripted gaits. Through AI and big-data training, DR01 can autonomously generate new behavioural skills as environments and tasks change. name: Adam
desc: Adam is the flagship full-size humanoid from Beijing-based PNDbotics, a full-stack developer of modular humanoid platforms (project started June 2023). Standing about 1.6 m and weighing ~60 kg, Adam is driven by 25 proprietary PND quasi-direct-drive (QDD) force-controlled actuators delivering up to ~360 N·m of leg torque, and is notable as one of the first humanoids with a biomimetic pelvis for more natural, stable gait. An Intel i7 (NUC) plus PND Robot Control Unit runs a deep-reinforcement-learning and imitation-learning stack trained in NVIDIA Isaac Gym with sim-to-real transfer, giving human-like walking, terrain traversal and disturbance recovery. Its modular, standardized architecture (with an open SDK) lets developers swap actuators, end-effectors and compute. Adam has had a high-profile demo run — playing keytar live at the VOYAGEX music festival, synced dancing at WAIC 2025, and completing the 100 m obstacle race at the 2025 World Humanoid Robot Games as the only full-size humanoid to finish. Prototype pricing is around US$120,000; sibling variants include Adam Lite, Adam-U (data-collection) and Adam SP.

name: MagicBot Z1
desc: The MagicBot Z1 is MagicLab's compact, high-agility bipedal humanoid, unveiled in July 2025 and shown again at CES 2026. At about 1.4 m (136.9 cm) and 40 kg it has a human-child footprint that slips through tight indoor spaces, with 24 degrees of freedom in the standard build expandable to ~50 when fitted with optional sensors, arms and the 11-DOF MagicHand S01 (which adds five-fingered grasping up to ~3-5 kg per arm). In-house high-torque joints exceed 130 N·m with up to 320 degrees of travel, giving it acrobatic agility — fast motion, deep back-bends, and fall/prone recovery under disturbance. A 360-degree sensor suite (3D LiDAR, depth and binocular fisheye cameras, head tactile sensing) feeds a VLN navigation stack, with Wi-Fi 6 / Bluetooth 5.2, an 8-core CPU and a quick-release 10,000 mAh battery good for ~2 hours. MagicLab markets it as an open, developer-friendly platform for research, education and dynamic applications; its full-size sibling MagicBot Gen1/G1 targets industry. No public price.

name: Isaac 1
desc: Isaac, from Weave Robotics (San Francisco, YC S24, founded 2024 by ex-Apple engineers who led Siri and shipped Apple Watch Double Tap), is a wheeled dual-arm home robot built to automate everyday chores — making beds, sorting clutter, folding laundry and putting things away. Deliberately un-humanoid to reach the home faster than general-purpose bipeds, it rolls on a motorized wheeled base and is fingerless (grippers, not hands), with a telescopic body that rises from about 0.9 m stowed to 1.75 m to reach furniture, beds and shelves. Its rounded head with expressive digital eyes and fabric-covered panels are tuned for living spaces. The key idea is hybrid autonomy: Isaac runs autonomously most of the time, but when it hits a task it can't finish, a remote human operator briefly teleoperates via its camera feeds and then hands control back — ensuring reliability across messy real homes. Cameras physically disable via hardware controls for privacy, and capabilities expand through OTA updates. It launched at $7,999 (or $449/month), succeeding the stationary laundry-folding Isaac 0, with California deliveries from fall 2026. name: GoMate
desc: The third-generation embodied-intelligence humanoid from Chinese automaker GAC (Guangzhou Automobile Group), unveiled December 2024. Its signature is an industry-first variable wheel-leg base that switches between a stable four-wheel mode (1.4 m tall, for stairs, slopes and obstacles) and an agile two-wheel mode (1.75 m tall, smaller footprint) — a design GAC says cuts energy use by over 80%. It has 38 DOF driven by in-house axial-flux joint motors (up to 1000 N·m) and coin-sized servo drives, an all-solid-state battery good for ~6 hours, GAC's pure-vision autonomous-driving algorithm plus FIGS-SLAM for centimetre positioning, and cloud multimodal AI for millisecond voice response. Pilot use began 2025 with small-scale production targeted for 2026.

AI HybridSense navigation (27 sensors incl. cameras + ultrasonics) builds a pool map and targets high-debris zones; dual brushes, a 5 L debris basket (150um+250um dual filter), dual LED night cleaning and self-parking at the pool edge. ~3.5 h runtime, 4-5 h charge.
cleaning_coverage: 5-in-1: surface + floor + walls + waterline + water clarification

name: Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus
desc: The Maytronics Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus is a popular corded robotic pool cleaner (~8.6 kg) with dual scrubbing brushes, a large top-load filter, wall-climbing and CleverClean navigation, plus app scheduling on the CC Plus model. 60 ft anti-tangle swivel cable for in-ground pools.
app: None (2019 base; CC Plus Wi-Fi variant exists)

name: S2 Solar
desc: The WYBOT S2 Solar is a solar-powered autonomous surface pool skimmer that floats and continuously collects leaves and debris from the water surface, recharging from the sun for hands-free daily skimming.
battery_type: Rechargeable, with floating solar charging dock

name: HOBOT-S6 Pro
desc: A premium window-cleaning robot from Taiwan's HOBOT (a window-bot pioneer since 2010), and the first with a patented dual-mop reciprocating polish — two cleaning cloths vibrating 600 times a minute over a 4 mm stroke to lift dirt and neutralise static for longer-lasting shine. Dual ultrasonic nozzles atomise water into 15 µm mist (about 1.3 ml per m²) for streak-free cleaning, while Edge-Leakage-Bumper sensors handle framed and frameless glass. Caterpillar treads move at 12 cm/s, cleaning 1 m² in ~2.6 minutes, with a UPS holding position for 20 minutes on power loss.

name: Litter-Robot 4
desc: The Whisker Litter-Robot 4 is a self-cleaning automatic litter box that sifts and rotates to separate waste after each use, with OmniSense weight/litter-level sensing that tracks each cat's weight and litter level, reporting to the Whisker app over Wi-Fi.

name: Grillbot
desc: A hand-sized automatic grill-cleaning robot that scrubs a barbecue grill at the push of a button. Three independent motors drive spinning brushes (available in brass, nylon or steel) inside a heat-resistant shell, moving in a random spin-stop-restart pattern for even coverage. An LCD timer offers 10, 20 or 30-minute cycles, and it runs on hot or cold grills. Powered by a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.
actuator_type: 3 motors driving 3 replaceable cleaning brushes

name: Tertill
desc: The first robotic weeder for home gardens, created by Roomba co-inventor Joe Jones at Franklin Robotics (later Tertill Corp) in North Billerica, Massachusetts. This solar-powered, weatherproof disc lives in the garden from spring to fall, using capacitive bumper sensors to tell tall plants from short weeds and a spinning nylon string trimmer to cut weeds at the base. Four-wheel drive with extreme camber wheels handles soil, sand and mulch; a physical garden border replaces any perimeter wire or GPS.
use_cases: Home garden weeding (up to ~200 sq ft)
actuator_type: 4-wheel drive, extreme camber wheels

name: Ghost (Anduril sUAS)
desc: Anduril's first drone: a soldier-portable, single-rotor helicopter-style VTOL small UAS built for quiet, modular ISR, targeting and force protection at the tactical edge. Running at low rotor speed for a near-silent acoustic signature, the ~17 kg Ghost 4 carries modular payloads — a Trillium EO/IR gimbal plus optional SIGINT, EW and radar — swappable in seconds, and is driven by Anduril's Lattice AI core (~3.2 TOPS) that enables full autonomy, sub-one-hour operator training, swarming and automatic 'battlefield handover' between aircraft for persistent coverage. Sold in pairs and packable in a backpack or Pelican case, two Ghosts give one operator round-the-clock ISR. The upgraded Ghost-X (2023) adds dual batteries, a tandem-rotor layout, vision-based GPS-denied navigation and far greater payload.
actuator_type: Single-rotor modular sUAS

name: HMND 01
desc: HMND 01, from London-based startup Humanoid, is a modular next-generation labor-automation humanoid engineered for industrial deployment with an explicit focus on low total cost of ownership. Standing 175 cm and 70 kg with 41 DOF, a 15 kg payload and 1.5 m/s walking speed, its standout trait is manipulation speed — hands that can move faster than a human's, via high-torque, high-speed self-developed actuators. Modularity is central: the upper body, lower body and end-effectors are interchangeable (a 12-DOF five-finger hand or a 1-DOF parallel gripper), and it comes in two Alpha forms — a bipedal version with an RL-trained whole-body controller (walking straight and curved, turning in place, sidestepping, backwards walking, squatting, hopping, running, with omnidirectional push recovery) and an omnidirectional wheeled version (up to 7.2 km/h). It runs Humanoid's KinetIQ framework (VLM + VLA based) for autonomous or teleoperated operation, with RGB plus dual depth cameras, a 6-mic array, and a head display with LEDs for multimodal interaction, and interchangeable protective garments for contamination control. Humanoid completed a bin-picking proof-of-concept with Schaeffler at its Erlangen site. NOTE: full specs from Humanoid official + humanoid.guide/QVIRO — verified; development-stage (Alpha prototypes 2025).

name: Oli
ai: LimX embodied AI stack — COSA, VGM, DreamActor, Agentic OS
desc: The LimX Oli is a full-size general-purpose humanoid robot from LimX Dynamics (Shenzhen), offered in four configurations — Oli Lite, EDU, Super and a taller 175cm model — sharing a common platform (following a GSMArena-style single-SKU-with-variants model). The 165cm models stand 165cm at ≤55kg with 31-33 DOF (6 per leg, 7 per arm, 3 waist, 2 neck); the 175cm flagship reaches 43 DOF, ≤60kg, 250 N·m peak torque, 5kg single-arm payload and a 9-axis IMU. All walk at up to 5 km/h and offer interchangeable end effectors (2-finger 1-DoF gripper, 3-finger 4-DoF gripper, or 5-finger 6-DoF dexterous hand). Compute scales from dual RK3588 (motion control) on the Lite/EDU to added NVIDIA Orin NX (157 TOPS) perception on Super/175cm, with an optional AGX Orin computing backpack (275 TOPS). A 9,500mAh slide-out battery gives ~1.5-2h, and the platform includes head/chest/wrist/hip depth cameras, LiDAR (higher variants), Wi-Fi 6, 5G, gigabit Ethernet, voice interaction, OTA and a full developer API suite (remote-control, sensor, low- and high-level motion control). All specs verified from LimX's official Oli spec page and brochure (2026-06-25).

desc: The LimX TRON 1, launched October 2024, is billed as the world's first multi-modal biped robot — a compact all-terrain research platform with a unique 'Three-in-One' modular foot-end design that switches between point-foot, sole, and wheeled configurations for different locomotion research. It runs a 12th-Gen Intel Core i3 (16GB/512GB), with electric joint actuators (48V, 30 N·m rated / 60 N·m peak, 15 rad/s), a swappable 240Wh ternary-lithium battery (~2h, <1h fast charge), IMU, optional RGBD camera, and GbE/USB 3.0 expansion. Offered as a $15,000 Standard Edition and $25,000 Education Edition (which adds secondary-development/SDK support for Python/C++ with Isaac/MuJoCo/Gazebo simulation). It's positioned as the gateway platform for humanoid motion-control and RL research. All specs verified from LimX's official TRON 1 spec page.

Its wheel-legged base carries 30kg on flat ground (20kg stair-climbing) at up to 5 m/s, climbing 30° slopes and 20cm steps. desc: The LimX P1 is LimX Dynamics' point-foot biped research robot, first shown March 2024 — the one-off experimental predecessor to the commercial TRON 1. Built as a platform for systematic reinforcement-learning development, P1 famously navigated the wild terrain of Shenzhen's Tanglang Mountain using zero-shot learning (trained purely in simulation, with no forest/hiking data), demonstrating dynamic locomotion and push/kick recovery over unpredictable ground. It moves up to 0.5 m/s, carries ~10 kg, and runs an Intel Core embedded computer with an RGBD camera and IMU, supporting Gazebo, MuJoCo and Isaac Gym simulation. As an internal research prototype it has limited published specifications; unpublished fields are flagged for outreach rather than guessed. Verified from LimX's official P1 materials.

name: Elektro
desc: Elektro, built by Westinghouse in 1937-39 and starring at the 1939 New York World's Fair, is one of the most famous early humanoid robots — a 2.1-metre (7-foot), ~120 kg gold-finished machine that captured the public imagination decades before modern robotics. Driven by electric motors, relays and photoelectric cells, it could walk on command (triggered by voice through a telephone-style link that converted words to relay pulses), speak a roughly 700-word vocabulary played from 78-rpm records, move its arms and head, count on its fingers, distinguish red and green light via photocells, and even 'smoke' a cigarette. It appeared with a robot dog, Sparko. Though it was a showcase automaton rather than an autonomous robot, Elektro is a landmark in the cultural and engineering history of humanoids. name: Theseus
desc: Claude Shannon’s maze-solving mechanical mouse — one of the first machine-learning devices ever built. Theseus explored a 25-square maze by trial and error, then "remembered" the solution using telephone relay circuits under the maze floor.

name: Unimate
desc: The Unimate is the world's first industrial robot — conceived by George Devol (who patented 'Programmed Article Transfer' in 1954) and commercialised by Joseph Engelberger through Unimation, with the first unit installed on a General Motors die-casting line in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961. A roughly 1,800 kg hydraulic arm with polar-coordinate motion (~5 axes) and a magnetic-drum memory that stored taught positions, it could lift heavy die-cast parts (payloads into the hundreds of kilograms) and perform spot welding on automobile bodies — dangerous, repetitive jobs it took over from human workers. The Unimate launched the entire industrial-robotics industry, made GM assembly lines the proving ground for automation, and led directly to Unimation's later PUMA. NOTE: The Unimate predates modern spec documentation; figures here reflect the historical record (payload ~227 kg / ~500 lb class, hydraulic drive, magnetic-drum control) and are intentionally limited to verified historical facts rather than a reconstructed datasheet.
actuator_type: Hydraulic actuators; magnetic-drum program memory

name: Shakey
desc: The first mobile robot that could reason about its own actions (1966–72). Shakey perceived its world with a TV camera and bump sensors, planned with the STRIPS algorithm, and rerouted around obstacles — work that produced A* search, computer vision foundations and modern AI planning.
actuator_type: Wheeled base, radio link to SDS-940 mainframe

name: WABOT-1
desc: WABOT-1, completed in 1973 at Waseda University under Professor Ichiro Kato ('father of Japanese robotics'), is recognised as the world's first full-scale anthropomorphic (humanoid) robot — the machine that began the entire quest to build robots in human form. It integrated, for the first time in one platform, quasi-static bipedal walking (keeping its centre of mass inside the support polygon), object grasping and transport with human-finger-mimicking hands, a stereo-camera vision system that measured distance and direction to objects, and a conversation system that recognised and responded to simple spoken Japanese through an artificial voice. Researchers compared its overall ability to that of a 1½-year-old child. Hydraulically driven and slow, it could only walk on flat surfaces — but it proved humanoid robots were possible and jump-started the field worldwide. It's on public display at Waseda's Nishi-Waseda campus. name: WABOT-2
desc: WABOT-2, introduced in 1984 by Waseda University's Kato laboratory, was the world's first musician humanoid robot — a 50-degrees-of-freedom machine that could read a printed musical score with its CCD-camera head and play a Yamaha FX-1 electronic keyboard using both hands and feet, even adjusting its performance to accompany a human singer. Its five-fingered hands with 3-DOF fingers performed precise, delicate keypresses, driven by DC motors and harmonic drives. Its distributed computing was remarkable for 1984: a 16-bit Zilog Z8001 for high-level limb control, two Z8002s for mid-level control while playing, and fifty 8-bit Z8094 CPUs — one dedicated to each degree of freedom — for low-level motor control. WABOT-2 demonstrated that humanoids could perform artistic, dexterous, real-time tasks, not just walk. NOTE: historic entry from Waseda archives and the robotics record — verified specs; overall mass/height not consistently published (flagged).

Work began in 1980; WABOT-2 was introduced in 1984 as a humanoid with musical ability, and became famous at Expo '85 in Tsukuba, Japan. A 50-DOF humanoid, it could read sheet music with a camera eye and play an electronic keyboard with both hands and feet - an early demonstration of perception + fine motor coordination. It usually resides beside WABOT-1 at Waseda.

name: Stanford Cart
desc: A pioneering self-driving vehicle research platform. In its famous 1979 run under Hans Moravec, the Cart crossed a chair-filled room entirely autonomously in about five hours, using stereo TV vision processed by a remote mainframe — ancestral DNA of every modern autonomous vehicle.
use_cases: Early autonomous navigation & computer vision research

name: PUMA 560
desc: The PUMA 560 (Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly) is one of the most historically important industrial robots ever built — developed by Victor Scheinman at Unimation in 1978, together with General Motors, and considered the archetypal anthropomorphic robot arm. Its six all-rotational axes with a 3R spherical wrist (2.5 kg payload, 864 mm reach, ~±0.1 mm repeatability, DC servos under Unimation's VAL controller) made it the reference manipulator for a generation of robotics research: its kinematics and Denavit-Hartenberg parameters appear in countless textbooks, and it remained a laboratory and teaching standard for decades. It shipped in a family (PUMA 260, 560, 761) and cemented Unimation — founded by robotics pioneer Joseph Engelberger — as the birthplace of industrial robotics. NOTE: The PUMA predates modern datasheet practice; specifications here are drawn from the published academic and historical record (Unimation documentation, robotics literature) rather than a current manufacturer datasheet — depth is intentionally capped to verified historical figures rather than invented.
actuator_type: DC servo motors with encoders (VAL controller)
controller: Unimation VAL / VAL II controller (DEC LSI-11)

name: Skilam SCARA
desc: The Sankyo Seiki Skilam is one of the first commercial SCARA robots — the SCARA concept (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm) was invented by Professor Hiroshi Makino at the University of Yamanashi around 1978-1981, and Sankyo Seiki was among the pioneering manufacturers (with the Makino lab) to commercialise it as the Skilam line. The SCARA's defining trait is selective compliance: rigid in the vertical (Z) axis but compliant in the horizontal plane, making it ideal for vertical insertion and assembly tasks — peg-in-hole, screwdriving, electronics placement — at high speed. This 4-axis architecture (two horizontal rotary joints, a vertical Z, and end rotation) became one of the two dominant industrial-robot form factors worldwide, and virtually every modern SCARA (Epson, Stäubli TS2, Denso, Yamaha) descends from this lineage. NOTE: The original Skilam predates modern datasheet publication; this entry documents the historically verified milestone and architecture rather than inventing per-axis figures — specific payload/reach numbers for the original model are logged as outreach rather than guessed.
actuator_type: Servo-driven horizontal articulated arm + vertical Z + rotation
configuration: SCARA (2 revolute X-Y + prismatic Z + rotary wrist)

name: HERO 1
desc: One of the earliest consumer/educational robots — the Heathkit Educational RObot (model ET-18), begun in 1979 and released in 1982, sold as a build-it-yourself kit ($1,500) or assembled ($2,500) with ~14,000+ units shipped. HERO 1 is a self-contained mobile robot on a Motorola 6808 8-bit CPU (1 MHz) with 4 KB RAM and 8 KB ROM, driven by seven stepper motors plus a DC drive motor across a three-wheel base whose head rotates 350 degrees to aim its sensors and optional arm. Onboard light, sound, ultrasonic-motion and Polaroid sonar sensors, an optical encoder and a real-time clock let it perceive its world; an optional five-axis arm/gripper and Votrax SC-01 speech synthesizer added manipulation and voice. Programmed in 6808 machine code via a 17-key hex keypad, a record/replay Teaching Pendant, or an IBM-PC ANDROTEXT compiler, with cassette-tape program storage. It even starred on TV's 'Mr. Wizard's World'.
actuator_type: 7 stepper motors + DC drive motor

name: RB5X
desc: A cylindrical, R2-D2-esque personal robot from RB Robot Corporation (Golden, Colorado; founded by Joe Bosworth in 1982) — one of the earliest commercial autonomous mobile robots and among the most durable personal robots of the 1980s (still manufactured today by RB Robotics). Under a clear domed top, RB5X runs a National INS8073 microprocessor with on-chip TinyBASIC and 8K of memory (expandable to 16K), programmable in TinyBASIC or Savvy and downloadable from any home computer over its (dual) RS-232 interface. It rolls at ~4 in/sec on two drive wheels and two casters, sensing the world with eight perimeter bump panels, a photodiode and a Polaroid sonar rangefinder (10 in to 35 ft). It learns from experience, finds its own charging nest when low, and offers an optional five-axis arm (lifts ~1 lb) and voice synthesizer. Sold in Germany as 'Toby'.

name: Armatron
desc: An iconic early-1980s robotic-arm toy from Tomy that introduced a generation to robotics and mechanical engineering. Entirely mechanical — a single electric motor drives an intricate gear train — it is operated by two joysticks that command multiple simultaneous motions: base rotation, shoulder and elbow articulation, wrist rotation and a grasping claw. A built-in countdown timer challenged users to complete pick-and-place tasks, and it ran on batteries with no electronics or programming. A celebrated example of purely mechanical multi-axis control.
actuator_type: Single electric motor + mechanical gear train

name: Omnibot
desc: An iconic 1980s programmable home robot from Japanese toymaker Tomy. Using a built-in cassette-tape deck, Omnibot could record and play back sequences of movements and speech, letting owners program it to roll around, speak and serve drinks from its front tray. It featured a wheeled base, remote control and a built-in clock/alarm, and became one of the most recognisable consumer robots of the personal-robot craze.
actuator_type: Wheeled drive base

name: Genghis
desc: Rodney Brooks’ six-legged insect robot that changed robotics philosophy: no world model, no central planner — just layered "subsumption architecture" behaviors that let a 1 kg machine scramble over rough terrain. Its DNA lives on in every behavior-based robot since.
actuator_type: 12 servo motors

name: Cog
desc: Cog was a landmark embodied-AI research humanoid built by Rodney Brooks's group at the MIT AI Lab from 1994 — an upper-body robot (torso, head, two arms; ~22 DOF on a fixed base) created to test a radical hypothesis: that human-like intelligence can only emerge from a human-like body interacting with the world, not from disembodied computation. Cog had foveated saccading stereo-camera eyes, vestibular and auditory sensing, and joint force sensing (an early platform for series-elastic actuation), and it learned behaviours like reaching, orienting to stimuli and rudimentary social interaction. It was hugely influential — a training ground for researchers including Cynthia Breazeal (who built the expressive robot Kismet nearby) — and shaped the embodied-cognition and social-robotics movements. Notably, Brooks went on to co-found iRobot and later Rethink Robotics (Baxter/Sawyer). NOTE: historic research entry from MIT records — verified specifics; some exact figures (mass, precise DOF by generation) vary and are flagged, not invented.

name: P2
desc: Honda's P2, unveiled December 1996, is one of the most important robots in history — the world's first self-regulating, autonomous, wireless bipedal humanoid, and the machine that stunned the robotics world and launched the modern humanoid era. At 1,820 mm and 210 kg with 30 degrees of freedom, it was the first to build everything — computer, motor drives, battery, and wireless radio — into its own torso, freeing it from tethers. It could walk autonomously at 2 km/h, climb up and down stairs (using a six-axis force sensor in its feet to estimate tread depth), push carts, and tighten bolts via a force-reflecting master arm. P2 directly led to ASIMO four years later, was recognised as an IEEE Milestone in 2026, and was loaned to Japan's AIST in 1998 to kick-start the national Humanoid Robotics Project (HRP). NOTE: specs from Honda's official robotics history and the IEEE Milestone record — this is a historic entry documented to verified figures, not a current datasheet.

name: P3
desc: Honda's P3, completed September 1997, is considered the world's first completely independent (fully self-contained) bipedal humanoid walking robot — the final prototype before ASIMO. Honda shrank it substantially from the P2: 1,600 mm and 130 kg (down from 210 kg) with 28 degrees of freedom, achieved by revising component materials and adopting a distributed control system, bringing it closer to a size that could blend into human living spaces. It walked autonomously at 2 km/h, climbed stairs, and pushed carts. The P3 was the direct bridge to ASIMO (2000), and its lineage also seeded AIST's HRP-1. name: Kismet
desc: A landmark of social robotics built in the late 1990s at MIT by Dr. Cynthia Breazeal as an experiment in affective computing — a robot head that could recognise and simulate emotion. Kismet perceives auditory, visual and proprioceptive social cues and responds with human-readable expressions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise, interest, calm, tiredness) through movements of its ears, eyebrows, eyelids, lips and jaw, plus expressive 'proto-speech' babble and tone of voice. Its active-vision system has four DoF (each eye pans independently, with a shared tilt), and the whole platform runs ~21 actuators fed by four cameras and three microphones across a network of computers. Funded by NTT and DARPA, Kismet now resides at the MIT Museum.
actuator_type: Servo motors (ears, eyebrows, eyelids, lips, jaw, eyes, neck)
display_face: Animatronic face (ears, eyebrows, eyelids, lips, jaw)

name: Furby
desc: The 1998 Furby — an owl/hamster-like animatronic toy from Tiger Electronics (designed by Dave Hampton and Caleb Chung) that became a cultural phenomenon, selling over 40 million units in three years. About 11 inches tall in synthetic fur, it produced 300+ movement combinations — blinking eyes, wiggling ears, an opening beak and a rocking body — all from a single motor driven through a camshaft gear assembly, a clever cost-saving feat for its time. A 6502-class microprocessor with only 128 bytes of RAM ran everything. Light, sound and touch sensors (in a touch > sound > light hierarchy) plus a tilt sensor let it react to its environment, and an infrared port between its eyes let two Furbies 'talk'. It started out speaking only 'Furbish' (42 root words forming 300+ phrases) and appeared to 'learn' English through play — a simulated effect, not real machine learning.
actuator_type: Single motor + camshaft (eyes, ears, beak, body)

name: MINDSTORMS RCX
desc: The brick that launched LEGO Mindstorms in September 1998 and effectively created the mass-market home-robotics kit. The RCX (Robotic Command eXplorer) grew out of a long LEGO / MIT Media Lab collaboration inspired by Seymour Papert's 'Mindstorms', and shipped as the heart of the Robotics Invention System (RIS 1.0, $199). The yellow programmable brick runs a Renesas H8/300 microcontroller (16 MHz) with 32 KB ROM and 32 KB RAM, exposing three sensor input ports and three 9V motor output ports plus an LCD. Programs are written on a PC (visual RCX Code, or community languages like NQC and leJOS Java) and beamed over infrared; two bricks can even talk to each other via IR. It anchored the first FIRST LEGO League season and built a huge hacker/education community before the line ended in 2022.

name: PaPeRo
desc: NEC's 'Partner-type Personal Robot' — a cute, toddler-sized companion robot developed from 1997 (as the R100 prototype) and named PaPeRo in 2001, one of the earliest robots built purely around the human-machine interface rather than locomotion or labour. Standing 385 mm and weighing 5 kg on a three-wheel base, it roams the home looking for faces using twin CCD-camera 'eyes' with facial recognition (identifying ~10 people), then starts a conversation. Four microphones let it locate and understand speech (recognising ~650 commands and speaking ~3,000 phrases), nine capacitance touch sensors sense patting and stroking, and ultrasonic, floor, lift and bumper sensors handle navigation. An expressive LED face (in eyes, mouth, cheeks and ears), stereo speakers, a wireless modem and TV/cellphone links round it out. Never sold publicly, PaPeRo ran for years in NEC's eldercare and smart-home experiments and spawned Childcare, PaPeRo 2005, Mini and Petit variants.

name: QRIO
desc: Sony's compact entertainment humanoid (originally the SDR-4X II prototype), announced in September 2003 as a successor to the AIBO robot dog. At 58 cm and ~7 kg with 38 degrees of freedom, QRIO used ZMP control to walk, dance and recognise faces, and in 2003 became the world's first humanoid capable of sustained running (~23 cm/s) — a feat recognised by Guinness World Records in 2005. It could also recover from falls. Sony ended the project in 2006.
actuator_type: Custom small actuators (developed for QRIO); ZMP-based balance control; force sensors in each foot; palm pressure sensor; pinch detection
manufacturer_history: Sony - originating in the SDR (Sony Dream Robot) project (started ~1997/2000 under Yoshihiro Kuroki at Sony Entertainment Robot Co. / Sony Intelligence Dynamics Laboratory). Prototypes SDR-0/1/2/3X/4X led to SDR-4X II, renamed QRIO ('Quest for cuRIOsity') in Sept 2003. On Dec 18, 2003 QRIO became the world's first humanoid robot to run (both feet off the ground) with an internalized power + control system. Never commercialized (~100 units); Sony ended development Jan 26, 2006, the same day it discontinued AIBO.

name: myCobot 320

Like its smaller sibling it packs the controller into the base — M5Stack or Raspberry Pi 4 depending on variant — and runs the same open software stack: Python through the open-source pymycobot API, Blockly's graphical interface for beginners, C++ and ROS. The end-effector ecosystem is its practical strength: adaptive grippers, a compressor-driven air parallel gripper for heavier grips, suction pumps and camera flanges mount to the standard interface, supported by AI vision kits for machine-learning coursework. It slots into Elephant's broader platform alongside the myAGV mobile base for mobile-manipulation teaching. name: Baxter
cameras: Head camera + cameras in each hand; sonar head sensors; IR hand ranging (Research Robot model)
actuator_type: Series Elastic Actuators (SEA) — spring at every joint absorbs impact & enables back-drive
desc: Rethink Robotics' Baxter (2012) was a landmark in collaborative robotics — the robot that popularised the idea of a fenceless, teach-by-demonstration arm that ordinary factory workers could program by grabbing and moving it. Designed by iRobot co-founder Rodney Brooks, it has a humanoid form: two 7-DOF arms (2.2 kg payload, 1,210 mm reach), a torso, and an animated LCD face that signals intent. Its defining technology is the Series Elastic Actuator — a spring at every joint that both senses force and physically absorbs impact, letting it work safely alongside people without cages under ISO 10218, and back-drive easily when pushed. It runs Intera on ROS from a PC in its chest, with cameras and sensors in its head and hands. The Research Robot variant (added head camera, sonar, IR, and an open SDK) became a fixture in university labs worldwide and seeded a generation of manipulation research. Priced around US$25,000, Baxter is discontinued (Rethink ceased operations in 2018, the brand later acquired), but its influence on cobot design endures. desc: Rethink Robotics' Sawyer (2015) was the more precise, single-arm successor to Baxter — a 7-DOF collaborative arm weighing just 19 kg with a 4 kg payload, 1,260 mm reach, and ±0.1 mm repeatability, designed to fit into work cells built for humans and reach where the larger dual-arm Baxter couldn't. Rethink redesigned its signature Series Elastic Actuators with a titanium spring and added Harmonic Drive servos and zero-backlash gearboxes, so Sawyer could 'feel' its way into fixtures and machines even when part positions varied slightly — the compliant-motion 'adaptive repeatability' that set Rethink apart. An embedded Cognex vision camera in the arm powers its Robot Positioning System for quick reorientation and redeployment, and it programs by zero-force hand guiding or the Intera 5 visual environment, on ROS with an open SDK. Certified ISO 10218-1 / PL d Cat. 3 for fenceless use and priced around US$29,000, Sawyer targeted machine tending, circuit-board testing and electronics assembly. Discontinued after Rethink ceased operations in 2018; the brand and Sawyer line were subsequently acquired and relaunched.

desc: BigDog (2005) was Boston Dynamics' pioneering DARPA-funded rough-terrain quadruped — a gasoline-powered, hydraulically actuated robot the size of a large dog, designed to carry ~150kg of load for soldiers over terrain too rough for wheeled vehicles. actuator_type: 12 pneumatic actuators (air servo valves + air servo control system embedded in body; small external compressor); chosen for very human-like, smooth, quiet motion

desc: Geminoid F ('F' for female), unveiled in 2010 by roboticist Hiroshi Ishiguro (ATR and Osaka University) with animatronics firm Kokoro, is one of the world's most famous ultra-realistic androids — a copy of a real woman in her twenties, with silicone skin and real human hair over a fiber-reinforced-plastic skull. Its design breakthrough was efficiency: where the earlier Geminoid HI-1 (Ishiguro's own copy) used about 50 actuators and a large external compressor box, Geminoid F achieves a convincing 'toothy' smile and a frown with just 12 pneumatic actuators concentrated in the face. It autonomously breathes and blinks, but to fully 'come alive' it's teleoperated: motion-capture software tracks a human operator's facial expressions and head movements and mimics them on the android in real time. It cannot walk — it's always seated — and exists to study human-robot interaction and the nature of 'human presence,' even appearing in theatre productions. It sits within Ishiguro's celebrated android family (Geminoid HI series, Repliee Q1/Q2, Telenoid, Erica). desc: Nadine, unveiled in 2015 at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, is a lifelike social android modelled on Professor Nadia Magnenat Thalmann — a pioneer of 'virtual humans' who directed NTU's Institute for Media Innovation and founded the University of Geneva's MIRALab. Its realistic hardware (silicone skin, articulated hands for natural grasping) was built by Japanese animatronics firm Kokoro, while Thalmann's NTU team created the software that gives Nadine her defining qualities: a personality and emotional range, the ability to make eye contact and shake hands, and — unusually — a memory that lets her recognise people she's met and recall previous conversations. Designed as a receptionist or a social companion for people with special needs and the elderly, Nadine became a widely-cited example of socially intelligent androids, conceptually akin to Ishiguro's Geminoids in being modelled on its own creator. name: Poppy
actuator_type: ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL
desc: Poppy, created by INRIA's Flowers team in Bordeaux (born 2012 out of Matthieu Lapeyre's PhD under Pierre-Yves Oudeyer, funded by an ERC grant), is the first complete open-source, 3D-printed humanoid robot — a platform designed so scientists, students, engineers and artists can fast and flexibly explore robot morphologies. About 840 mm tall and only ~3.5 kg, it has 25 DOF driven by Robotis Dynamixel servos, including a distinctive 5-DOF articulated trunk that gives it lumbar-spine-like motion unusual among humanoids. Both hardware (Creative Commons, 3D-printed skeleton, Arduino/Raspberry-Pi electronics) and software (GPL, the Python PyPot library plus a Snap block-based web interface, with V-REP simulation) are fully open, so its mechanical design can be freely modified — it was even reproduced in a two-day workshop at a Paris science museum. Widely adopted in schools and universities across science, education and art, Poppy's compliant Dynamixel control enables soft, safe human-robot interaction. The team later spun out Pollen Robotics, creators of the Reachy open-source humanoid torso. NOTE: specs from INRIA/Poppy Project official + academic papers — museum-grade open-source sourcing (v1 figures; the platform is intentionally variable).

desc: The VR-H3, from VinRobotics (a subsidiary of Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup), is the company's third-generation industrial humanoid — a pioneer of Vietnam's entry into industrial humanoids, unveiled at ICRA 2026 in Vienna and COMPUTEX Taipei 2026. Standing about 178 cm and 75-85 kg, it uses more than 31 smart motors driving rotary joints that mimic human kinematics for fluid walking, gesturing and object manipulation in crowded or hazardous factory environments, with each arm lifting around 3 kg. VinRobotics developed the key technologies in-house — mechanical structure, computing platform, battery management, electrical architecture and AI control software — and demonstrated VR-headset teleoperation with built-in motion capture requiring no external trackers.
