name: D1
desc: The D1 from Hong Kong's Direct Drive Technology is billed as the world's first fully modular embodied-intelligence robot. Two wheel-legged biped units (24.3 kg each) dock via a central magnetic coupler to form a 48.6 kg wheel-legged quadruped 'robot dog', then separate again autonomously - a capability the company calls 'All-Domain Splicing'. Each unit runs an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (8 GB) on Ubuntu 22.04, powered by a 43.2 V / 9 Ah battery good for over five hours, and can roll at up to 11 km/h or walk over rough terrain. Combined, the quadruped carries up to 100 kg (80 kg when standing), with a 25 km empty-load range, targeting security patrol, last-mile delivery, search-and-rescue and mobile filming. A single biped unit is US$7,499; the two-unit quadruped is US$13,999.

desc: KAI is a full-size humanoid robot from Shenzhen startup Kinetix AI (Kai Robotics), unveiled in April 2026 and aimed at retail, concierge and home-assistance roles rather than heavy industry. Priced from about ¥39,900 (~US$5,500), it targets education, research, elder care and developer use, and helped triple Noetix's valuation amid 2,500+ pre-orders.

name: Onero H1
desc: The SwitchBot Onero H1, unveiled at CES 2026, is a wheeled dual-arm home robot from SwitchBot — the smart-home-gadget maker's boldest move into humanoids, pitched as 'the most accessible AI household robot' at around $1,500. Standing 1.3 m on a wheeled base (chosen for stability and cost over legs), it has two articulated arms with 22 degrees of freedom — in Atlas's ballpark (29 DOF) for a fraction of the price — driven by SwitchBot's self-developed OmniSense VLA (vision-language-action) model that fuses visual, depth and tactile data to handle small, contact-heavy household tasks without meticulous pre-programming. Demos show it folding laundry, washing dishes, serving coffee, washing windows and loading washing machines, doing some tasks itself while delegating complex ones to task-specific devices in SwitchBot's Smart Home 2.0 ecosystem. It poses a genuine strategic question: specialised single-purpose devices, or one adaptable generalist? A companion A1 standalone robotic-arm product accompanies it. raw_specs.ecosystem_role: Orchestrator — does some tasks itself, delegates complex duties to task-specific SwitchBot devices (vacuums, purifiers, humidifiers)
raw_specs.availability: Pre-orders on SwitchBot official site; price not yet announced; concept/direction-signal, not mass-ready

name: Kata Friends
desc: Kata Friends are SwitchBot's line of fluffy AI companion robots, launched in 2026 in two characters — Noa and Niko. Each is a soft, palm-friendly desktop creature with large expressive digital eyes and a camera 'nose', designed to see, listen and learn through speech, touch and vision. The robots respond to handling and conversation, recognise faces and read emotional cues, building a personalised relationship over time as part of SwitchBot's broader smart-home ecosystem. Positioned as approachable, pet-like companions rather than task robots, the Kata Friends target everyday emotional engagement, family interaction and play.

name: Acemate Tennis Robot
desc: The Acemate Tennis Robot (model S10) is billed as the world's first AI tennis robot built for real rally play — a TIME Best Invention of 2025 that began shipping in early 2026 after a multi-million-dollar Kickstarter. Unlike static ball machines that just feed balls, the Acemate moves around the court on four omnidirectional Mecanum wheels at up to 5 m/s, tracking shots with dual 4K binocular cameras and reacting in just 0.15 seconds to catch your return in its net and rally back with spin, slices and lobs (up to ~80 mph and 8 m high). A swappable 6,700 mAh battery gives about three hours of play and holds up to 80-130 balls. Its companion app (V2.0) offers 40+ structured drills, 20 programmable target zones, real-time shot heat maps, ITN-aligned assessments, AI coaching tips and Apple Watch biofeedback sync. Priced from US$2,499 (Basic Kit) / $2,899 (Premium), it created a new category of mobile AI training partners.

name: Dragon Runner 20
desc: Compact, rugged man-portable tracked robot carried in a backpack and deployable in seconds for reconnaissance, inspection and light EOD in confined spaces. The DR20 can be fitted with a manipulator arm; its smaller sibling, the throwable DR10, provides immediate situational awareness. Widely used by NATO EOD and dismounted units, including extensive UK service.
cameras: Front tilting day camera + motion/sound sensors (detect to ~9 m)

name: Mission Master CXT
desc: Rugged 4x4 diesel-electric hybrid UGV built for extreme terrain, carrying its full 1,000 kg payload with advanced amphibious capability. Combines a diesel engine with a silent electric motor for a 450 km total range (including 50 km battery-only), and is internally transportable by CH-47, CH-53 and C-130 aircraft. Shares the Mission Master autonomy and C2 suite with the rest of the family.
navigation: Follow-me, convoy, waypoint (PATH A-Kit); wolfpack multi-UGV control
armament: Optional Fieldranger Multi RWS w/ twin M134D Minigun (counter-UAS + fire support)

name: Mission Master XT
desc: Rugged 4x4 high-mobility A-UGV based on the Zeal Motor Fat Truck platform, carrying up to 1,000 kg without compromising amphibious capability and offering a 750 km range. Integrated Li-ion batteries give around six hours of silent-watch endurance, and the design follows NATO STANAGs and US MIL-STD-6017 for battle-management interoperability. Can be parachute-delivered and underslung by CH-53/CH-47, with built-in cyber and electronic-warfare resilience.
cameras: 360° awareness: LiDAR, radar, cameras + ultrasonic proximity
armament: Modular fire-support: twin-M134 Minigun RCWS, Spike NLOS, Fieldranger, loitering-UAS module

name: Hunter WOLF
desc: Rugged 6x6 hybrid-electric squad support UGV (Wheeled Offload Logistics Follower) built to carry heavy loads, evacuate casualties and mount a remote weapon station for overwatch. Fielded by US Army units including the 101st Airborne Division, where it has been operated with a remotely-controlled .50-calibre machine gun during combat training. Designed for last-tactical-mile resupply and dismounted-squad support in GPS-degraded environments.
power_source: Hybrid diesel/JP-8 electric; 20 kW generator (15 kW export)
armament: Remote weapon station up to 30 mm autocannon (live-fire tested); M2 .50 cal option

name: MUTT 8x8 (S-MET)
desc: 8x8 Multi-Utility Tactical Transport selected as the US Army's Squad Multipurpose Equipment Transport (S-MET) program of record. Carries roughly 1,000 lb (454 kg) of a dismounted squad's load, lightening soldiers' burden, and provides 3 kW (stationary) / 6 kW (moving) of exportable power to recharge radios and batteries. Operates in tethered follow-me, teleoperation and waypoint modes.
customers: US Army (S-MET Program of Record, Increment I)
power_source: Diesel-electric hybrid; exportable power (3 kW stationary / 1 kW moving)

name: Arion-SMET
desc: 6x6 multipurpose unmanned ground vehicle for transport, reconnaissance, surveillance and casualty evacuation, with autonomous follow-me, remote control and waypoint navigation plus voice/gesture command features. Hanwha's Arion-SMET took part in a US Army Foreign Comparative Testing (FCT) program, demonstrating logistics and squad-support roles for international evaluation.
customers: US Army & USMC (Foreign Comparative Test, Hawaii 2023)
cameras: EO/IR ISR suite; gunshot source localization
armament: DNN RCWS — 5.56 mm extendable to 7.62 mm MG; gunshot localization + return fire
navigation: Autonomous off-road, tether-follow, autonomous homing on comms loss, MUM-T

name: REX MK II
desc: Wheeled infantry combat-support UGV from IAI's ELTA division, designed to accompany dismounted troops carrying gear, ammunition and water, evacuate casualties and act as a mobile sensor and weapons platform. Operated by remote control or follow-me autonomy and integrated with battle-management systems for networked operations.
armament: RCWS — 7.62 mm MG and .50 cal (12.7 mm) HMG
navigation: Fully autonomous with C2, or remote operation; MUM-T (demo'd with BAE Systems)

name: tEODor EVO
desc: Latest evolution of the heavy-duty tEODor (telerob Explosive Ordnance Disposal and observation robot), originally built by Telerob of Germany and now part of AeroVironment. A rugged tracked EOD platform with automatic tool-change capability for identifying and disarming IEDs, booby traps and unexploded ordnance in buildings, vehicles and confined areas. More than 450 of the tEODor family serve in 41 countries, trusted by 20 NATO nations.

name: ANDROS Mark V-A1
desc: Large, highly stable ANDROS variant used as the US military's Remote Ordnance Neutralization System (RONS) for the most demanding hazardous-duty operations. Its variable-speed manipulator lifts up to 100 lb and offers dual-sided quick-change accessory mounts, while a sealed weather-resistant enclosure and articulating tracks let it work in harsh environments and cross ditches and obstacles.
cameras: Color pan/tilt surveillance cam (216:1 zoom, 26x optical/12x digital, image-stabilized), stationary arm cam (40:1, 10x optical/4x digital), 24in camera extender

name: Uran-9
desc: Tracked unmanned ground combat vehicle for remote reconnaissance and fire support of infantry, unveiled at Army-2016 and entering Russian service in 2019. Roughly 10 tonnes, 5.12 m long, with a 35 km/h road speed and a remotely operated turret carrying a 30 mm 2A72 autocannon, coaxial 7.62 mm MG, four 9M120 Ataka ATGMs and six Shmel-M thermobaric rockets. Combat-tested in Syria, where reports highlighted control-link dropouts and inability to fire on the move, limiting effective control range to about 3 km.
armament: 30 mm 2A72 autocannon (350–400 rpm), 7.62 mm PKTM coax MG, 4x 9M120 Ataka ATGM, 6x Shmel-M; optional Igla/Strela SAM
cameras: EO/IR with laser rangefinder & FCS; auto target detection (tanks 6 km day / 3 km night)
navigation: Remote control + column autonomy; mobile command post
manufacturer_history: Developed by JSC 766 UPTK, now Kalashnikov Concern; marketed internationally by Rosoboronexport.

name: Uran-6
desc: Light tracked robotic mine-clearance system weighing up to six tonnes, designed to breach minefields and conduct area demining while keeping sappers away from direct contact with ordnance. Fitted with interchangeable mine-clearing implements (rollers, flails, ploughs) and operated by remote control. Used by Russian engineering units for explosive-remnant clearance.
blast_rating: Designed to survive anti-personnel & light anti-tank mine detonations

name: Platform-M
desc: Compact tracked combat robot of around 800 kg, armed with a 7.62 mm machine gun and rocket-propelled grenade launchers for reconnaissance, patrol and fire support. Issued for experimental operation to Russian Navy coastal troops in Kaliningrad and Kamchatka, it can be operated by remote control to engage stationary and moving targets.

name: Marker
desc: Modular experimental UGV developed by Android Technics and Russia's Advanced Research Foundation as a testbed for autonomy, machine vision and swarming. Built in tracked and wheeled configurations with a modular payload bay that can mount machine guns, anti-tank missiles (Kornet) or loitering-munition launchers, it is used to mature group-control and autonomous-navigation technologies for future Russian combat robots.
armament: Modular: MGs, Kornet ATGM, loitering-munition launchers

name: Sharp Claw 1
desc: Small lightweight (~120 kg) tracked scout-and-strike UGV designed for anti-terror, patrol and urban-battle missions, able to climb stairs and clear buildings and tunnels. Armed with a 7.62 mm machine gun (effective to ~500 m) and a sensor package for all-round surveillance, controlled by radio to ~800 m. Designed to be carried in the cargo bay of the larger Sharp Claw 2; confirmed in PLA service and reportedly deployed to the Tibetan border with India.
deploy_method: Carried in Sharp Claw 2 cargo bay
navigation: Remote control; can be carried & deployed by Sharp Claw 2

name: Sharp Claw 2
desc: Larger 6x6 electrically-powered UGV with a combat weight up to 1,000 kg and a 50 km range over a four-hour period, able to carry and deploy the smaller Sharp Claw 1 to extend operational reach. Features independent suspension for high cross-country mobility (climbs 0.35 m obstacles, 30% gradients), a 7.62 mm machine gun and a mast-mounted surveillance package, plus autonomous path-tracking on a digital map.
navigation: Autonomous path-tracking on digital map; remote control

name: Sharp Claw VU-T2
desc: Compact multi-role tracked combat UGV unveiled by NORINCO at UMEX 2026, designed for combat support, reconnaissance and direct engagement under remote control or in coordination with crewed platforms. The shown configuration mounts a 12.7 mm machine gun module and a BA-5 missile launcher, with a multi-sensor perception architecture fusing LiDAR, EO cameras, radar and inertial navigation with digital maps for semi-autonomous navigation and target detection.
armament: 12.7mm machine gun module + BA-5 missile launcher
navigation: Semi-autonomous: LiDAR + EO + radar + INS sensor fusion with digital maps

name: Droid TW 12.7
desc: Compact Ukrainian tracked reconnaissance-and-strike UGV mounting a remotely operated turret with a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun. Top speed about 7 km/h and operational range up to 25 km, with an AI-assisted fire-control package that stabilises the weapon, tracks targets and computes ballistic solutions while a human keeps the trigger decision. In December 2025 a Droid TW 12.7 destroyed a Russian MT-LB armoured carrier near Kostyantynivka — the first documented case of a Ukrainian ground robot killing an enemy armoured vehicle — and another reportedly held a position for 45 days.
armament: 12.7mm M2 Browning HMG on remote weapon station
cameras: Thermal + EO gun sight; AI-assisted fire control (stabilisation, tracking, ballistic solution)
encryption: Digital radio (MikroTik); mesh / LTE / Starlink resilient links

name: Droid NW 40
desc: Reconnaissance-and-strike UGV from DevDroid adapted to carry a 40 mm automatic grenade launcher (Mk-19 or AGL-53) on a remote weapon station for high-risk fire-support missions without exposing personnel. It passed Ukrainian Ministry of Defence codification and received a NATO stock number, clearing it for official supply to Ukraine's Security and Defence Forces.
encryption: Digital radio; mesh / LTE / Starlink options

name: Ironclad
desc: Armored combat UGV from Roboneers — whose roots trace to the 2014 volunteer-built ShaBlya remote weapon turret — designed for assault operations and fire support on the front line. Carries a stabilised remote weapon station (commonly a 7.62 mm machine gun) on a protected wheeled/tracked chassis, letting operators suppress positions and support advancing infantry from cover.
armament: ShaBlya M2 remote weapon station (7.62 mm MG; stabilised)
manufacturer_history: Roboneers' remote-turret work traces to the 2014 volunteer-built ShaBlya station.

name: Lyut
desc: Machine-gun-armed combat UGV produced by Ukrainian Unmanned Technologies, whose work traces back to 2016 volunteer development in the ATO zone. Built for remote fire support and position defence on the front line and fielded alongside the company's Ravlyk logistics platform within Ukraine's fast-iterating UGV ecosystem.
manufacturer_history: Traces to 2016 volunteer development in the ATO zone; fielded alongside the Ravlyk logistics UGV.

name: TERMIT
desc: Multifunctional tracked support UGV codified by Ukraine's Ministry of Defence in June 2025, able to carry up to 300 kg across rough terrain, slopes, obstacles and trenches. Its low tracked profile suits routes where wheeled supply vehicles are too visible, and it reconfigures for medical evacuation, logistics resupply, mine-laying and equipment transport for front-line units.

name: Daksh
desc: Electrically powered, remotely operated wheeled vehicle developed by India's DRDO to locate, handle and destroy IEDs and other hazardous objects. Its robotic arm lifts and scans suspect objects with a portable X-ray, defuses them with a water-jet disrupter, and a 12-gauge shotgun can break open locked doors. Climbs stairs up to 40°, negotiates steep slopes and narrow corridors, carries an RF jammer to block trigger signals, and a RADMAC unit for NBC contamination survey. About 90% indigenous; the Indian Army ordered 20 with larger follow-on orders.
encryption: Wireless 500 m / fibre-optic 100 m control link

name: Daksh Mini
desc: Lightweight version of the Daksh ROV developed for confined-space operations, designed to work inside aircraft, trains and buses where the full-size bomb-disposal robot faces mobility limits. Retains the family's remote IED-handling and inspection capability in a smaller, more agile package.

name: Daksh Scout
desc: Compact reconnaissance-and-explosive-handling member of the Daksh family, developed for rapid deployment and surveillance. Built to scout ahead, inspect suspect objects and support EOD teams with a smaller, quick-to-deploy platform.

name: Cameleon E
desc: Modular lightweight UGV from France's ECA Group for EOD, IEDD and CBRN missions, with a 25 kg payload and a plug-and-play architecture that swaps cameras, jaws and disruptors in the field. Its six-axis manipulator reaches 1.5 m vertically and 1.2 m horizontally and lifts about 8 kg; an onboard X-ray, day/night ISR cameras, a 5 m audio microphone and optional jammer, radio relay and 200 m fibre-optic drum round out the kit. Combat-proven over a decade, including with the French Army's Operation Barkhane in the Sahel and with French and Hungarian police.
cameras: Day/night ISR cameras + onboard X-ray; 5 m audio microphone
hand_type: 6-axis manipulator (1.5 m vertical / 1.2 m horizontal reach, ~8 kg lift)
encryption: 200 m fibre-optic drum + radio (optional relay & jammer)

name: COBRA MK2 E
desc: Modular lightweight UGV from ECA Group built specifically for EOD and IEDD operations, designed for fast deployment in confined and hard-to-reach areas. Shares the Cameleon family's plug-and-play payload approach with a smaller, more portable chassis for rapid render-safe tasks.

name: CUTLASS
desc: Latest-generation EOD unmanned ground vehicle designed, developed and built by Northrop Grumman in the UK, descended from the Wheelbarrow bomb-disposal lineage. Features a high-dexterity nine-axis manipulator and multiple onboard cameras for precise render-safe work against IEDs and CBRN threats, with secured digital control and high-quality video out to around 1 km.
cameras: Multiple onboard cameras (high-quality video to ~1 km)
manufacturer_history: Descends from the Wheelbarrow bomb-disposal lineage; built in the UK.

name: Miloš
desc: Tracked armed-reconnaissance UGV from Serbia's Military Technical Institute, first shown at Partner 2017 with a remote weapon station carrying a Serbian M86 7.62 mm machine gun (effective to 800 m) and a 40 mm automatic grenade launcher (effective to 400 m). The 360°-traverse RWS pairs with a CCD day camera, low-light camera, thermal imager and laser rangefinder. Weighs 620 kg, runs about an hour on internal batteries, manages 7 km/h, and can pivot on its own axis for tight urban spaces. Can swap the combat module for an ATGM in the anti-tank role.
cameras: CCD day camera + low-light camera + thermal imager + laser rangefinder

name: Miloš L
desc: Logistics-and-rescue configuration of the Miloš family, shown at Partner 2025 in Belgrade as an unarmed pack-mule and casualty carrier. The tracked platform carries up to 250 kg — several combat loads or a casualty-extraction sled with basic medical gear — at up to 10 km/h with a zero-radius turn, running about three hours on electric drive. Compact enough for a light utility vehicle to carry, with camera-based navigation and a portable control console.

name: BARKAN
desc: Autonomous armed UGV from Turkey's Havelsan, introduced in early 2021 with a remote-controlled weapon station, electro-optical sensors and multiple data links. Its modular design supports armed ISR, close protection and armed reconnaissance, giving field units stealthy, agile fire support and multi-sensor intelligence as part of Havelsan's 'digital troops' concept.
manufacturer_history: Part of Havelsan's 'digital troops' concept; BARKAN family inducted into Turkish service in 2023.

name: BARKAN 3
desc: Most advanced member of the BARKAN family, unveiled at SAHA 2025 with a 12.7 mm weapon system, front-driving and ground-facing cameras, a 25 km/h top speed and five hours' operation at full load. Designed for AI-enabled swarming — demonstrated in mixed swarms of eight units and intended to scale to dozens — and integrated with Havelsan's ADVENT-AI decision layer and Baha/Bozbey UAVs for manned-unmanned teaming in contested electronic-warfare environments. The BARKAN family first entered Turkish service in 2023.
navigation: AI swarm; MUM-T with Baha/Bozbey UAVs

name: Vision 60
desc: Mid-size, high-endurance all-weather quadrupedal UGV (Q-UGV) built for force protection, perimeter patrol, surveillance and CBRNE reconnaissance across unstructured urban and natural terrain. Weighs 51 kg, carries up to 10 kg of modular payload on MIL-STD-1913 rails, rated IP67 and -40 to 55 °C, with five surround cameras and perception-aided stair climbing and obstacle avoidance. Walks at 1 m/s up to a 3 m/s sprint, with roughly 3 hours of continuous walking or 21 hours standby. The US Air Force fielded V60s with Tyndall's 325th Security Forces Squadron in 2022, and DHS trialed them on the southern border.
cameras: 5x RGB surround cameras + 4x depth; optional thermal & LiDAR
ethernet: Managed GigE switch (supports 5G, SDR, SATCOM, Silvus, Persistent, Rajant)
navigation: 3D LiDAR SLAM; GPS-denied capable; point-and-click waypoint
ai_model: Deep-learning object detection (API); blind-mode biomimetic control core
actuator_type: 3-DOF quick-change leg pods (proximal motors)
deployed_at: US Air Force — Tyndall AFB, 325th Security Forces Squadron

name: Agema
desc: Fully modular, multi-mission tracked UGV from UAE-based Milanion Group, designed to be fast and adaptive across roles from ISR and fire support to logistics, casualty evacuation and counter-mobility. Accepts a range of mission payloads including remote weapon stations, anti-tank missiles and mortar systems, making it a flexible building block for unmanned ground formations.

name: HR-Sherpa
desc: Multipurpose wheeled (6x6) unmanned ground vehicle from Hyundai Rotem of South Korea, designed for surveillance and reconnaissance, supply transport, casualty evacuation and fire support. Electrically driven with autonomous follow and remote-control modes, it can mount a remote weapon station and is part of Korea's push toward manned-unmanned teaming for its ground forces.

name: Cameleon LG E
desc: Latest light-segment addition to ECA Group's Cameleon UGV range, built for EOD/IEDD and reconnaissance where a small, quickly deployed platform is needed. Shares the family's modular plug-and-play payload architecture and intuitive operator interface, compatible across ECA Group's wider UGV line for shared payloads and reduced acquisition cost.

name: REEM-C
desc: A full-size bipedal research humanoid from PAL Robotics with 68 degrees of freedom, built as a fully-ROS platform for navigation, vision, whole-body-control and human-robot-interaction research. REEM-C walks stably up to 2.5 km/h, climbs stairs, sits, and lifts 10 kg with both arms. It ships with out-of-the-box skills — walking, grasping, whole-body control, text-to-speech in 30+ languages — and runs standard Ubuntu LTS for open development.
use_cases_note: Full-size biped research platform (locomotion, HRI, navigation)
manufacturer_history: PAL Robotics (Barcelona; part of PAL Technology Group, Abu Dhabi/UAE; founded 2004; CEO Francesco Ferro). REEM-C (2013) was PAL's first commercially available bipedal humanoid and one of its most influential products - an adult-size ROS research platform. Lineage: REEM-A (2005, walk + play chess) -> REEM-B (2008, 12 kg payload) -> REEM/REEM-H (2010, wheeled service) -> REEM-C (2013). PAL also makes TALOS, TIAGo, ARI and Kangaroo.

name: HRP-5P
desc: HRP-5P, unveiled by AIST in 2018, is the strongest and most autonomous member of Japan's HRP humanoid series — a prototype construction robot built to take on heavy, hazardous building labour amid Japan's shrinking workforce. At 1,820 mm and 101 kg with 37 DOF (the most in the HRP series: 2 neck, 3 waist, 8 per arm, 6 per leg, 2 per hand), it uses high-power motors — several per joint on heavy-load axes — to autonomously locate, lift and carry large drywall/plaster panels and screw them to walls with power tools. A 3D head sensor maps its surroundings for object detection and navigation. AIST shed the futuristic shells of earlier HRP robots for a purely functional industrial body, positioning HRP-5P as an industry-academia R&D platform for practical humanoid use in constructing buildings and large structures like aircraft and ships. NOTE: full DOF breakdown and mass/height from AIST's official announcement; historic entry, verified figures.
actuator_type: High-power motors + drive-mechanism cooling; some joints powered by multiple motors; high-power wide-range electric joints
manufacturer_history: AIST (National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology), Japan, with Kawada Industries; team led by Fumio Kanehiro. HRP-5P (unveiled 2018) is the 5th-generation HRP humanoid - built with a robust body + advanced intelligence to autonomously perform heavy labor or work in hazardous environments, a response to Japan's aging-population labor shortage. Demonstrated autonomous drywall installation. Aimed at building construction and large-structure assembly (aircraft, ships).
vision: 3D environment mapping head sensor; object recognition
capabilities: Autonomous construction labor: locates, lifts and carries drywall/plaster board and screws it to walls using power tools; aimed at building & large-structure (aircraft/ship) assembly
developed_by: AIST (team led by Fumio Kanehiro)

name: HRP-2 (Promet)
desc: HRP-2 (Promet), unveiled in 2002, is one of the most influential research humanoids ever built — the flagship of Japan's national Humanoid Robotics Project (AIST with Kawada Industries and Kawasaki Heavy Industries, under NEDO/METI). At 1,540 mm and 58 kg with 30 DOF, it introduced a capability ASIMO famously lacked: the ability to get up unaided after lying flat on its back or front, plus cooperative heavy-object lifting with humans, walking on uneven surfaces, crawling through tight spaces, and sitting/standing. Its distinctive futuristic shell was designed by anime mecha artist Yutaka Izubuchi. HRP-2 became a widely-used research platform at labs in Japan and abroad and defined the HRP series' role as an open R&D humanoid. NOTE: historic entry from AIST/Kawada and IEEE Spectrum robot records — verified figures, not a current datasheet.
actuator_type: Electric servo motors; cantilevered crotch/hip structure; FEM-designed rigid links; internal ventilation cooling
manufacturer_history: AIST (National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Humanoid Research Group) + Kawada Industries (Tadahiro Kawada) + Yaskawa Electric, as the final platform of Japan's METI Humanoid Robotics Project (HRP, 1998-2002). HRP-2 'Promet' (announced 2002) was the first human-size robot able to lie down and get back up. Its distinctive futuristic exterior was designed by anime-mecha designer Yutaka Izubuchi. Succeeded by HRP-3 (2006), HRP-4/4C (2009-10), HRP-5P (2018).
capabilities: Cooperative heavy-object lifting with humans; walking on uneven surfaces; get-up from lying (back or front) — a first vs ASIMO; crawling through tight spaces; sit/stand
design_note: Futuristic exterior by anime mecha designer Yutaka Izubuchi
developed_by: AIST + Kawada Industries + Kawasaki Heavy Industries (NEDO HRP project)

name: NEXTAGE
desc: NEXTAGE, from Kawada Robotics (developed out of the HRP program), is a dual-arm production humanoid designed to work alongside people on assembly and production lines. Rather than a walking biped, it's a human-upper-body form on a fixed base: two 6-DOF arms, a 2-DOF head and a 1-DOF torso (15 DOF total), with stereo cameras in its head and a camera in each hand for vision-guided precision assembly. Built for collaborative deployment in the same spaces as human workers — no fences — it targets electronics assembly, precision production, machine tending and kitting, and became one of Japan's most recognisable factory humanoids. It shares engineering DNA with the Kawada/AIST HRP walking robots but is aimed squarely at practical manufacturing. name: TOPIO
desc: TOPIO (TOSY Ping Pong Playing Robot), developed from 2005 by Vietnamese firm TOSY and famously debuted at the Tokyo International Robot Exhibition in November 2007, is a bipedal humanoid built to play table tennis against human opponents — a striking, sci-fi-looking demonstration of fast robotic manipulation and vision. The flagship TOPIO 3.0 stands 1.88 m and weighs 120 kg on a carbon-fiber-composite frame for quick reactions, with 39 DOF driven by brushless DC servo motors (the line evolved from the 20-DOF hydraulic TOPIO 1.0 through the 42-DOF TOPIO 2.0 to 3.0). It tracks the ball's trajectory and spin with four high-speed cameras and two processing units, using predictive motion planning to return shots, and an AI system that learns and improves its play over time — it can even record scores and express emotions mid-game, sustaining rallies of a few turns. TOSY also made a 40 cm 'Tiny TOPIO' and the wheeled service robot TOPIO Dio. name: K-Bot
desc: K-Bot, from K-Scale Labs (Palo Alto), is billed as America's first open-source full-size humanoid robot — a developer- and community-driven platform in deliberate contrast to closed commercial humanoids. At launch its software provides the fundamentals: standing, walking, balancing and obeying simple commands, controllable via a mobile app or voice. Because it's internet-connected and fully open-source, K-Bot is designed to gain new skills continuously through software updates from K-Scale and the open community, with the company committing to free upgrades for early buyers until the robot reaches full autonomy — defined as handling most tasks independently with under one human intervention per day. K-Scale's roadmap integrates vision-language-action AI so K-Bot can follow complex natural-language instructions, targeting broad autonomy by around 2028. It's aimed at developers, makers, educators and autonomy researchers who want an open platform to build on. NOTE: K-Scale publishes an open-source spec/hardware repo; exact height/weight/DOF/actuator figures vary by build and are flagged for outreach rather than guessed here — open-source status, control methods and roadmap confirmed from K-Scale.

name: Phantom MK1
desc: The Foundation Phantom MK1 is a camera-first industrial and defense humanoid from San Francisco startup Foundation Robotics (founded 2024 by CEO Sankaet Pathak). Standing 1,750 mm at ~80 kg, it carries 20 kg continuously (up to 36 kg peak) and walks at 1.7 m/s. Its core differentiator is a proprietary cycloidal actuator — up to ~160 N·m, back-drivable and impact-resistant, offering hydraulic-like torque with electric efficiency and human-safe compliance — technology inherited when Foundation acquired Boardwalk Robotics in December 2024 (Boardwalk's upper-body 'Alex' platform became the Phantom). Rather than LiDAR, it uses an 8-camera camera-first perception system feeding an LLM-driven task-to-motion stack: large language models reason over natural-language commands like 'pick that up,' proprietary physics-action models generate the motion, and a shared world graph coordinates fleets. With 19 upper-body DOF and anthropomorphic five-fingered hands, it targets assembly, inspection, logistics and reconnaissance in near-24/7 operation. Over 40 units were built by December 2025, and in February 2026 two units were sent to the Ukrainian frontline — believed to be the first deployment of a humanoid to an active combat zone. An MK2 with ~30% more payload is slated for 2026. NOTE: 19 DOF is the published upper-body figure; full-body count and finger DOF/IP rating not yet public (flagged).

name: Rollin' Justin
desc: Rollin' Justin, from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), is a landmark mobile-manipulation research humanoid: a torque-controlled humanoid upper body — two 7-DOF DLR-Lightweight-Robot-III arms, two dexterous DLR-Hand-II hands and a 3-DOF movable torso — mounted on an omnidirectional wheeled platform with a variable, extendable base. The whole system weighs 199 kg and rolls on four independent hub-motor steering wheels (30 N·m each, 1.5 m/s, climbing 40 mm steps and 17° ramps). Its defining technology is DLR's modular drive concept: brushless-DC motors with harmonic-drive gears and link-side joint torque sensors on every joint, giving back-drivable behaviour and highly sensitive impedance control — the basis for safe physical interaction with people and delicate two-armed manipulation (famously demonstrated serving tea). It's a premier platform for autonomous dexterous mobile manipulation in human environments, with envisioned use in households and space (astronaut assistance), and sits in DLR's humanoid family alongside Agile Justin, the biped TORO and neoDavid. NOTE: specs from DLR official + the Rollin' Justin design papers (ICRA 2009) — verified research-grade sourcing; a mobile manipulator, recorded honestly as wheeled not biped.

name: Beomni 1.0
desc: Beomni 1.0, from Colorado Springs-based Beyond Imagination (led by CEO Harry Kloor), is a teleoperated wheeled humanoid built to enable remote work across geographic distance — letting a human operator perform complex physical tasks from anywhere without being present. It has a human-like upper body (articulated head, shoulders, waist and arms) with dexterous hands and opposable thumbs that can lift up to 15.88 kg (35 lb) per arm yet still perform delicate actions like pinching salt or opening a bottle, all on a four-wheel base that traverses mud, sand, snow and rough terrain. It's piloted via a VR headset and gloves with low-latency stereo vision, haptic feedback and 3D audio, while its AI brain learns from those demonstrations to progress toward semi- and eventually full autonomy. Beyond Imagination targets healthcare and eldercare especially, plus manufacturing and agriculture. NOTE: specs from Beyond Imagination + databases; recorded honestly as a teleoperated wheeled humanoid; exact total DOF/battery not uniformly published, flagged.

name: Reflex
desc: Reflex, from New York's Reflex Robotics, is a wheeled humanoid mobile manipulator — a dual-arm humanoid upper body on a wheeled base rather than legs, a deliberate choice (shared with Weave, Galbot and others) to reach real deployments faster and cheaper while sidestepping the reliability and cost burdens of bipedal balance. With a telescoping torso for variable working height, it targets practical tasks like logistics, material handling and general labor, and uses a teleoperation-to-autonomy pipeline: human operators guide the robot while the collected data trains increasing autonomy. Reflex positions the platform for fleet deployment in commercial settings. NOTE: Reflex publishes limited formal spec tables (exact DOF/payload/reach/battery) — those are flagged for outreach rather than guessed; the wheeled mobile-manipulator architecture, telescoping design and teleop-to-autonomy approach are confirmed.

Shown at Modex 2024 (Gen 2), it has run pilots with GXO. Human operators drive it immediately while AI learns from the demonstrations.

name: AEON
desc: The industrial humanoid from Hexagon Robotics — the new division of Hexagon AB, the $28B Swedish precision-measurement giant. AEON is a 1.65 m, 60 kg humanoid with 34 degrees of freedom and five-fingered hands that moves at up to 8.6 km/h and carries 15 kg. It folds Hexagon's metrology heritage into a mobile platform: a fused RGB/depth/LiDAR/force sensor suite captures centimetre-accurate reality data and digital twins that upload to Hexagon's Reality Cloud Studio. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin runs motion planning, spatial AI and edge LLM reasoning, with hot-swappable batteries for round-the-clock uptime. An NVIDIA GR00T ecosystem partner, AEON is piloting at BMW's Leipzig plant and is the subject of a 1,000-unit Schaeffler deployment commitment.

name: Kaleido 9 (RHP)
desc: The Kawasaki Kaleido 9, unveiled at iREX 2025 in Tokyo, is the ninth generation of Kawasaki's RHP Kaleido humanoid line (in development since 2015). At 1,900 mm and 99 kg, it's taller and heavier than earlier Kaleidos but far more capable: engineers significantly reinforced the waist and leg joints to solve the classic bipedal problem of balancing under load, enabling it to lift 30 kg. A new sensor suite — LiDAR plus enhanced stereo cameras — lets it build 3D maps and navigate autonomously in dynamic settings, and it supports VR remote control for disaster-response scenarios and can learn to operate tools like cleaning equipment. Kawasaki's roadmap targets simple factory tasks by 2030, complex assembly by 2040, and full disaster response beyond. It represents Kawasaki's bid to turn 50+ years of industrial-robot expertise into a practical working humanoid. NOTE: figures from Kawasaki official + iREX 2025 reporting; verified.

desc: Kawasaki's Kaleido (RHP — Robust Humanoid Platform) is the humanoid line from one of the world's oldest industrial-robot makers, in development since 2015 and first shown in 2017. This generation stands 1,780 mm at 85 kg with 32 DOF and unusually high industrial upper-body strength — handling loads up to 60 kg — while achieving fully untethered bipedal walking on an onboard battery. Kawasaki hit that stand-alone operation without weight gain through aggressive engineering: a magnesium-alloy skeleton (lighter than aluminium) and 3D-printed resin exterior panels replacing metal, plus integrating the previously external ~30 kg controllers into compact in-body drivers. It demonstrated stand-ups, pull-ups and two-handed grasping, with stereo-camera vision and object recognition. Kawasaki aims Kaleido at disaster response and dangerous industrial tasks, leveraging 50+ years of factory-robot heritage. name: Lingxi X2-N
desc: A hybrid-mobility variant of AGIBOT's compact Lingxi X2 (AGIBOT / Zhiyuan Robotics, Shanghai; the world's #1 humanoid producer by 2025 shipments), debuted at CES 2026 with a Tai Chi demonstration. The X2-N transforms its feet into wheels to switch between bipedal walking and wheeled rolling, using proprioceptive feedback — joint torque, pressure sensors and gyros rather than cameras — to adapt in real time, climb stairs and traverse ramps with light loads. It shares the X2 chassis (~1.31 m, ~35 kg, ~28 DoF) with AGIBOT's Xyber-Edge 'cerebellum' controller and Xyber-DCU decision unit, and is programmable through the ROS2-based AimDK_X2 framework in Python or C++.

name: Bumi
desc: The Noetix Bumi is a compact, consumer-priced bipedal humanoid from Beijing's Noetix Robotics — designed to bring genuine legged locomotion to classrooms, makerspaces and homes at a price previously reserved for wheeled toys. Standing 980 mm and about 17 kg with 21 DOF, it delivers stable walking, dynamic dance routines, voice interaction and a full graphical programming environment in a kid-safe, easy-to-carry chassis. Its proprietary N-shaped TIX force-controlled joint modules produce up to 70 N·m peak knee torque for stable walking and dynamic recovery, and it sees via a structured-light depth camera, running 2-3 hours per charge. Bumi gained international attention as one of four Chinese humanoids in China's 2026 Spring Festival Gala, performing live alongside human actors before 700M+ viewers — validating its reliability for unscripted interaction. It's the entry point to Noetix's lineup, sharing joint architecture with the larger N2 (which placed second in the world's first humanoid half-marathon), and ships in eight versions from Lite to Jetson-Orin-powered EDU-Max. NOTE: specs from Noetix/verified sources; the EDU-tier Jetson Orin is real (not a generic placeholder), confirmed per official version list.

name: Q5
desc: The RobotEra Q5 is a wheeled service humanoid from Beijing's ROBOTERA (founded 2023), a super-humanoid built for professional service scenarios. At 1,650 mm and 65 kg with 44 full-body DOF — including the agile 11-DOF XHAND Lite (StarMotion 'Elf Hand') for precise manipulation — it can squat to pick up objects, twist its waist, shake hands and lift up to 10 kg with a single arm. High-precision bionic 7-axis joints and harmonic-drive actuators give it smooth motion; a lithium battery with BMS powers it; and a sensor suite of Livox Mid-360 LiDAR, IMU, stereo RGB cameras and torque sensors drives LiDAR-visual fusion navigation. It supports full-body teleoperation through gloves and VR (plus 2.4G wireless), recognises 37+ languages, and learns new tasks from human demonstration videos, improving via a closed loop of teleoperation, data collection and model iteration shared with RobotEra's STAR1 platform. It targets commercial services, cultural tourism, hotels, elderly care and education. NOTE: full spec cross-verified from RobotEra official + databases (165cm/65kg/44DOF/10kg/XHAND-Lite 11-DOF).

desc: Roboy, from Devanthro (originating at TU Munich / Fortiss in 2013), is an open-source tendon-driven musculoskeletal humanoid built to mimic the human muscle-tendon system rather than use conventional rigid joints. Its 'myorobotic' actuation pairs electric motors with springs and tendons to emulate biological muscles, giving compliant, human-like movement, and the project has iterated through multiple generations exploring biologically-inspired robotics, telepresence avatars and prosthetics research. Devanthro develops Roboy as an open platform (ROS-based) with an active research and maker community, positioning it alongside other musculoskeletal efforts like Clone's Myofiber androids and the University of Tokyo's Kengoro. NOTE: Roboy exists in several research generations with varying configurations; Devanthro publishes limited fixed spec tables (exact DOF/height/weight vary by build) — those are flagged for outreach rather than guessed; the tendon-driven myorobotic architecture, open-source status and research focus are confirmed.

A digital face with expressive eyes handles interaction, and mobility plus elevation extend its working reach in 3D space. Shown as a development concept rather than a shipping product.

desc: Kangaroo, from Barcelona's PAL Robotics, is a bipedal humanoid robot purpose-built for research on agile and dynamic locomotion. Its signature engineering is mechanical: instead of conventional rotary joints, Kangaroo uses custom linear actuators with integrated force sensors arranged in closed/parallel kinematic chains, concentrating mass away from the legs to achieve very low moving inertia — which translates into high joint speeds and torques, better impact resilience and reduced energy consumption. It features 12 actuated degrees of freedom per leg and has demonstrated real-hardware jumping, showcasing the platform's robustness and resilience. PAL positions Kangaroo as a testbed for dynamic locomotion, reinforcement learning and embodied AI, complementing its established humanoid and mobile robots (TALOS, TIAGo, REEM, ARI). name: ergoCub
desc: ergoCub, from the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia (IIT), is an ergonomically-designed collaborative humanoid — an evolution of IIT's famous iCub — built specifically to reduce musculoskeletal injuries among workers. Standing 1.5 m and 55.7 kg and able to carry about 10 kg, its geometry was optimised during design to minimise the combined energy/joint effort of human-robot lifting tasks. It incorporates an Intel RealSense depth camera and LiDAR for navigation, new-generation force-torque sensors that let it respond intuitively to external forces, and a flexible OLED 2K face screen for expressive interaction, all powered by an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier alongside an 11th-gen Intel i7. It's the centrepiece of the ergoCub project, a collaboration between IIT and INAIL (Italy's workplace-accident insurer, which funded €5M over three years) aimed at cutting biomechanical risk for future workers through humanoids, wearables and AI. name: Origin
desc: Origin, from Chinese startup AheadForm, is an ultra-realistic expressive robotic head that startled viewers with facial movements many described as eerily human — blinking, glancing and shifting gaze with lifelike subtlety. Its two differentiators are a custom brushless-motor system — compact, quiet and energy-efficient, giving the fine control needed for subtle eyebrow raises and gaze shifts, potentially cheaper to scale than servo-and-linkage approaches — and self-supervised AI algorithms integrated with high-DOF bionic actuation to drive micro-expressions. Where Hanson Robotics' Sophia leans on Frubber skin and broad, recognisable expressions, AheadForm focuses on the fleeting nuances of real human movement, and its 'Elf series' deliberately adopts slightly stylised, elf-like features (large ears, exaggerated expressiveness) as a design choice. Origin targets human-robot interaction research, expressive avatars and engagement applications. Its standout technology is OptiMove — an intuitive motion-programming system that simplifies setup while improving repeatability and delivering the smoothest high-speed, high-payload motion in UR's line — running on the AI-ready PolyScope platform. TÜV and UL 1740 certified and suited to higher-IP environments, the UR15 keeps UR's signature ease of use, small footprint and rapid redeployment. It complements the tried-and-tested e-Series with the extra speed and payload the flagship UR Series is built for.

desc: The Universal Robots UR7e is the medium-duty member of UR's proven e-Series, delivering a 7.5 kg payload and 850 mm reach at ±0.03 mm repeatability from a compact 20.6 kg arm on a Ø151 mm footprint. Introduced in 2025 as a renamed, payload-upgraded successor to the UR5e (UR's best-selling size), it fills the gap between the UR3e and UR12e while keeping the e-Series' defining strengths: a built-in tool-flange force/torque sensor (±50 N / ±10 Nm, precision ±3.5 N), 21 configurable safety functions certified PL d Cat. 3, 4 m/s TCP speed, IP54 sealing, and any-orientation mounting. It runs UR's industry-standard PolyScope software on a 12-inch touchscreen with freedrive teaching and the vast UR+ ecosystem of certified end-effectors and apps, plus Modbus TCP, EtherNet/IP, PROFINET/PROFIsafe and ROS/ROS2. With over 100,000 UR cobots delivered worldwide, the e-Series is the reference platform for collaborative automation; the UR7e targets machine tending, assembly, screwdriving and inspection where reach and accuracy matter in tight cells.

It keeps the full e-Series platform: a built-in force/torque sensor (±50 N / ±10 Nm), 21 configurable PL d Cat. 3 safety functions, 4 m/s TCP speed, IP54 sealing, and any-orientation mounting, all programmed through PolyScope on a 12-inch touchscreen with freedrive teaching and the UR+ accessory ecosystem. Backed by the largest cobot install base in the world (100,000+ units) and the deepest third-party ecosystem, the UR12e is a workhorse for medium-to-heavy collaborative automation across industries.

name: CRX-5iA
desc: The FANUC CRX-5iA is the entry model of FANUC's CRX collaborative family — 5 kg payload, 994 mm reach, ±0.03 mm repeatability from a 25 kg arm light enough to install without a crane. Like every CRX it carries FANUC's signature reliability claim: 8 years of zero maintenance, backed by the company's industrial track record. Built-in torque sensing in every joint gives sensitive contact detection for fenceless ISO 10218-1 collaboration, and programming is deliberately novice-friendly — drag-and-drop icons on the Tablet Teach Pendant plus lead-through teaching, running on the compact R-30iB Mini Plus controller from standard single-phase power. Two J6 connection ports quick-change end-of-arm tooling, and the FANUC ecosystem (iRVision, force sensors, ROBOGUIDE simulation, ROS-Industrial) plugs straight in. A food-grade variant adds NSF-H1 grease, white epoxy paint and rust/chemical-resistant plating.

name: CRX-10iA
desc: The FANUC CRX-10iA/L is the long-reach variant of the 10 kg CRX — 1,418 mm reach with a unique underflip motion that swings the arm beneath its own base, maximising flexibility in tight cells where a conventional wrist path can't fit. It shares the family DNA: ±0.04 mm repeatability, 40 kg installable-by-hand mass, joint torque sensing for fenceless contact-stop collaboration, 8-years-zero-maintenance design, Tablet TP drag-and-drop programming, and the R-30iB Mini Plus controller on standard single-phase power. It's the basis of two notable specials: the CRX-10iA/L Paint — the first and only cobot approved for painting under U.S. safety standards, serving liquid/powder coating and fiberglass dispensing — and a food-grade version with NSF-H1 grease, white epoxy paint and rust/chemical-resistant plating.

Repeatability holds at ±0.04 mm, joint-level torque sensing provides the family's sensitive contact detection for fenceless ISO 10218-1 operation, and the 8-years-zero-maintenance design carries over. Programming stays drag-and-drop on the Tablet Teach Pendant with lead-through teaching, on the compact R-30iB Mini Plus controller. Dual J6 tooling ports, iRVision/force-sensor integration, ROBOGUIDE and ROS-Industrial complete the ecosystem, and a food-grade version (NSF-H1 grease, white epoxy, rust/chemical-resistant plating) serves wet and hygiene-critical environments.

name: LBR iisy 3 R760
desc: The KUKA LBR iisy 3 R760 is KUKA's accessible, plug-and-produce cobot — a 3 kg / 760 mm 6-axis arm at ±0.1 mm repeatability and 22.8 kg, built to get non-experts from unboxing to a running basic application in about 30 minutes. Integrated joint torque sensors make it sensitive enough for fenceless collaboration with hand guiding, certified PL d Cat. 3, and it's the entry point to a family spanning 3, 6, 8, 11 and 15 kg payloads. Its real platform advance is software: the LBR iisy runs KUKA's newest operating system, iiQKA.OS, on the compact KR C5 micro control box with the smartPAD-Pro, and the iiQKA 'Robotics Republic' ecosystem lets users bolt on grippers, vision and other components app-store style for rapid repurposing. KUKA leans on decades of industrial componentry for the durability claim, positioning the iisy as reliable industrial technology in an approachable collaborative package.

name: LBR iiwa 14 R820
desc: The KUKA LBR iiwa 14 R820 is the world's first series-produced sensitive robot — 'LBR' for Leichtbauroboter (lightweight robot), 'iiwa' for intelligent industrial work assistant — and one of the most influential research and HRC platforms ever made. Its defining feature is joint torque sensors in all seven axes, giving instant whole-arm contact detection with axis-specific torque accuracy of ±2% of maximum torque, so it can perform force-controlled contour-finding, delicate joining and compliant insertion without crushing or shearing hazards, fenceless, certified to PL d Cat. 3. The 14 kg / 820 mm redundant 7-axis arm weighs 29.9 kg, carries IP54 sealing, mounts in any orientation, and routes pneumatic and electrical supply internally to a DIN ISO 9409-1-50-7-M6 media flange. It runs from the KUKA Sunrise Cabinet, programmed in Java via Sunrise.Workbench or by hand guiding — and its 1 kHz Fast Robot Interface (FRI) made it the de-facto standard arm for robotics-research labs worldwide. A 7 kg / 800 mm sibling (LBR iiwa 7 R800) shares the platform.

name: GoFa 5 (CRB 15000)
desc: The ABB GoFa 5 is the founding model of ABB's GoFa CRB 15000 collaborative family — 5 kg payload across 950 mm wrist reach (1,050 mm to flange) with best-in-class ±0.02 mm repeatability and TCP speeds to 2.2 m/s, which ABB bills as roughly 50% faster than same-class cobots. Torque and position sensors in every joint drive SafeMove power-and-force limiting certified PL d Cat. 3 with up to 16 configurable safety zones, wrapped in rounded no-pinch geometry with an interaction status light. The 28 kg, IP54 arm on a 165×165 mm base mounts in any direction and runs from ABB's OmniCore controller with RobotWare 7 — programmed by grabbing the arm anywhere (lead-through), Wizard graphical blocks on the FlexPendant, RAPID, or RobotStudio offline with ~99% sim-to-real fidelity. The Ultra Accuracy option cuts path accuracy to 0.03 mm — over 10× tighter than rival cobots — for gluing, sealing and laser applications. ISO Class 4 cleanroom rated; Pro variant adds PROFINET.

Its IP67 sealing — a step above the GoFa 5's IP54 — suits dusty and moisture-prone floors across a 5–45 °C range, and the 51 kg arm on a ~200×200 mm base mounts in any orientation. The platform is pure GoFa: joint-integrated torque/position sensing feeding PL d Cat. 3 SafeMove with 16 configurable zones, interaction status light, grab-anywhere lead-through, Wizard blocks, RAPID and RobotStudio offline programming on the OmniCore controller. The Ultra Accuracy option (0.03 mm path / 0.1 mm absolute) opens sealing, laser welding and precision cutting across its wide envelope. ISO Class 4 cleanroom; Pro variant adds PROFINET.

name: SWIFTI CRB 1100
desc: The ABB SWIFTI CRB 1100 collapses the cobot/industrial-robot divide: built on the IRB 1100 industrial platform, it delivers a TCP speed above 5 m/s — five times faster than typical 4 kg cobots — and ±0.01 mm repeatability, up to ten times tighter than the collaborative norm, while remaining fenceless. Safety is speed-and-separation rather than contact-based: SafeMove paired with a safety laser scanner slows or halts the arm before a human can reach it, with an interaction light signalling status, certified PL d Cat. 3. The 4 kg / 580 mm arm (a 475 mm / 4.32 m/s variant exists) carries four integrated air supplies for vacuum grippers and runs from the OmniCore controller, programmed via a clip-on lead-through device, Wizard graphical blocks, the SafeMove Configurator app, RAPID or RobotStudio. It targets intermittent-collaboration tasks — assembly, kitting, polishing — where industrial speed matters but a human must occasionally step in.

name: PoWa
desc: ABB's high-speed collaborative-robot family, launched first for the Chinese market in July 2025 (built at ABB's Shanghai Mega Factory) and globally in 2026. PoWa - a name meant to evoke 'power' - closes the gap between light traditional cobots and rigid industrial robots, delivering industrial-grade speed and payload in a compact, fenceless package. The family spans six payload categories from 7 kg to 30 kg with a best-in-class top speed of up to 5.8 m/s and, ABB says, the longest reach and highest arm load in its class (7-10 kg on the lower arm / Axis 3, easing tool and cable mounting for arc welding). It runs ABB's OmniCore controller with built-in Power-and-Force Limiting and Speed-and-Separation Monitoring for safe shared workspaces, carries IP65/IP67 protection and ISO Class 4/5 cleanroom compatibility, and can be unboxed and running in about 60 minutes via no-code Wizard programming, arm-side buttons and plug-and-play tooling (RobotStudio / AppStudio).

name: Racer-5 COBOT
desc: The Comau Racer-5 COBOT is, by Comau's account, the only collaborative robot that automatically switches from full industrial speed to collaborative speed the instant a human operator enters its working area — letting one machine replace two (a fast industrial arm and a separate cobot). It pairs a 5 kg payload and 809 mm reach with ±0.03 mm repeatability and up to 6 m/s Cartesian speed in non-collaborative mode, throttling to ≤500 mm/s when collaborating, with Safe Collision Detection certified PL d Cat. 3 by TÜV Süd for fenceless operation. Made entirely in Comau's Turin plant with a rigid construction for lasting precision, it routes electrical and air connections at the forearm to avoid external harnesses, signals its mode via an LED status stripe, and offers Comau's arm-mounted MI.RA vision system for pick-and-place. A Racer-5-0.63 industrial variant (627 mm) completes the family, targeting automotive, electrification and general-industry assembly, dispensing and machine tending.

name: LS6-B SCARA
desc: The Epson LS6-B is a value-focused 4-axis SCARA robot built for factories that need reliable high-speed assembly at a budget price — 6 kg payload, up to 600 mm reach (500/600/700 mm arm lengths available), ±0.015 mm repeatability and a 200 mm Z-stroke, with high acceleration/deceleration for fast cycle times. Epson leans on its RC+ development environment (SPEL+ 7.0 language) and low-cost RC90 controller to make it easy to program, with integrated options for Epson Vision, fieldbus interfaces, teach pendants and customizable GUIs. An ISO 4 Clean version suits dust-critical and cleanroom applications. It targets the price/performance sweet spot for mechanical and electrical assembly, pick-and-place, kitting and dispensing where throughput matters and budget is tight — part of Epson's position as one of the world's highest-volume SCARA makers.
teach_pendant: Epson teach pendant (optional)

name: COBOTTA
desc: The DENSO COBOTTA, launched in 2018, is an all-in-one desktop collaborative robot built around portability and out-of-the-box simplicity — a 4 kg unit with the controller integrated into the arm, a 0.5 kg payload (0.7 kg with axis 5 vertical) and 342.5 mm reach, small enough to carry between benches. It targets labs, life-sciences and education, where its visually-oriented COBOTTA World tablet app lets non-programmers build pick-and-place tasks in minutes, while experts can use PacScript through the Remote TP virtual pendant or Python via ORiN/b-CAP. Safety is inherent-by-design with proprietary torque sensors monitoring torque and speed continuously on every axis, certified to ISO 10218-1 / ISO/TS 15066, and an electric gripper and 2D camera integrate directly onto the arm for force-controlled gripping and image-recognition tasks. Developed as an open platform, it slots readily into existing systems and has become a common research and laboratory-automation arm.

name: COBOTTA PRO 900
desc: The DENSO COBOTTA PRO 900 is the smaller of DENSO's high-speed PRO cobots — 6 kg payload, 900 mm reach, ±0.03 mm repeatability and a 2,100 mm/s TCP speed that puts it on par with 5- and 6-axis industrial robots during high-speed operation (the larger PRO 1300 pushes 12 kg and 2,500 mm/s). Its productivity-and-safety balance comes from proprietary high-rigidity torque sensors on lightweight slim axes for continuous torque/speed/area monitoring, plus a distinctive touch-sensing soft cover — silicon cushioning with embedded high-sensitivity contact sensors — that further cuts collision risk; with an added safety scanner it can safely ramp to industrial speeds when no one is near. DENSO reworked direct teaching so complex precision tasks like assembly can be memorised by track and fine-tuned to 0.1 mm, and paired it with a Blockly visual environment so novices can build high-precision applications. Pneumatic and I/O wiring route internally to the flange. NOTE: reach recorded as 900 mm per model designation; some aggregators list 1066 mm — flagged for datasheet confirmation.

name: MELFA ASSISTA (RV-5AS-D)
desc: The Mitsubishi Electric MELFA ASSISTA (RV-5AS-D) is Mitsubishi's collaborative robot, fusing the company's decades of industrial-robot experience with cobot-style ease of use — a 6-axis arm with 5 kg payload, 910 mm reach and a high ±0.03 mm repeatability at nominal load. It's designed to work hand-in-hand with people without fences or enclosures, using per-joint torque sensing for collision monitoring under ISO 10218-1 / ISO/TS 15066, an LED ring for at-a-glance status, and Direct Teaching buttons for point teaching without a pendant. Programming is deliberately open and intuitive via RT VisualBox's drag-and-drop visual environment (no-code), MELFA BASIC VI for depth, and RT ToolBox3, with a broad gripper and vision ecosystem including MELFA-Vision and the AI-driven MELFA SmartPlus option. Uncommon among cobots, it's engineered for food-safe environments, making it a fit for hygiene-sensitive pick-and-place, assembly, machine tending and inspection, as well as research and education.

name: CZ10
desc: The Nachi CZ10 is the collaborative robot from Nachi-Fujikoshi, one of Japan's oldest industrial-robot makers — a 6-axis, 10 kg-payload arm with a long 1,300 mm reach and ±0.08 mm repeatability, built on the company's welding and material-handling heritage. Its inherent-safety design maintains a 25 mm minimum clearance to prevent pinching, and torque sensors at every axis detect worker contact and stop the robot, third-party certified to ISO 10218-1 (plus TÜV and standard UL/CSA). An inline-wrist structure enables intuitive direct teaching, and wrist-integrated digital I/O (4 in / 3 out) with built-in φ4 air piping reduces installation wiring. The 61 kg arm carries IP65 protection (IP54 wire harness), operates 0–45 °C, runs at up to 180°/s joint speed (throttled to 250 mm/s in collaborative mode), and draws just 1.0 kVA with its CCZ controller. It mounts floor or inverted and targets machine tending, material handling, palletizing and dispensing.

name: YL012
desc: The Hyundai Robotics YL012 is the medium model of Hyundai's YL collaborative series — a 6-axis, 12 kg-payload cobot with a 1,305 mm reach, developed to operate directly alongside human workers. A Red Dot Design Award winner, its slim, organic, right-angle-free form isn't just aesthetic: all pneumatic, electrical and communication wiring is routed inside the arm joints for a clean profile that reduces snag points and interference in tight spaces, while cutting weight. LED flash lamps give 360° status visibility and an ergonomic handgrip with intuitive switches makes teaching quick and direct. It supports an unusually broad fieldbus set — PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, PROFIBUS, DeviceNet, CANopen, CC-Link (and IE Field), EtherCAT and Modbus TCP — for easy line integration, and its 12 kg reach suits palletizing, packaging, machine loading, polishing/deburring, gluing, injection-molding tending and inspection. A smaller YL005 (5 kg, 916 mm) completes the pair.

name: CR10
desc: The Dobot CR10 is the high-reach model of Dobot's CR collaborative series — 10 kg payload across a long 1,525 mm reach with ±0.03 mm repeatability, from Dobot, China's #1 cobot exporter. Built for affordability and fast deployment (about 20 minutes to set up, one hour to production), it uses a plug-and-play design with simple wiring and quick accessory access, running on DC 48 V with a 4 m/s TCP speed and all joints spanning ±360°. Safety is a strength: 22 built-in features certified to ISO 13849 and ISO/TS 15066, five adjustable levels of collision detection, and optional DOBOT SafeSkin technology giving 15 cm proximity sensing and active protection. It's programmed through DobotStudio Pro (graphical and script), with Modbus/PROFINET/EtherNet-IP connectivity and a 32,000-hour MTBF. Part of a CR family spanning CR3 to CR16, the CR10 targets palletizing, loading/unloading and heavy material handling. NOTE: reach recorded as Dobot's official 1,525 mm; some aggregators list 1,300 mm (an earlier-gen figure).

name: Nova 5
desc: The Dobot Nova 5 is a compact 6-axis collaborative robot with a 5 kg payload, 850 mm reach and a fine ±0.02 mm repeatability, designed by Dobot (China's #1 cobot exporter) for service, retail and light-industrial automation — it's a common choice for robotic coffee and beverage stations as well as light assembly and pick-and-place. It shares the Dobot cobot toolkit: adjustable collision detection with optional SafeSkin proximity sensing, IP54 sealing, electromagnetic brakes, and safety aligned to ISO 13849 / ISO/TS 15066, all programmed through the graphical DobotStudio Pro (plus script and Blockly) with Modbus, PROFINET and EtherNet/IP connectivity and a ROS driver. Its compact form and service-friendly design make it a fixture in customer-facing automation and education. name: ReBeL
desc: The igus ReBeL is the world's first cobot built around plastic strain-wave gears — a radical cost-and-weight play from the German motion-plastics specialist. At just 8.2 kg with a 2 kg payload, 664 mm reach and ±1 mm repeatability, it deliberately trades precision for affordability and low mass, using igus's self-lubricating tribo-polymer components in integrated joints (motor + strain-wave gearbox + absolute encoder) to hit a price point that opens robotics to SMEs, educators and developers. It runs from 24 V DC through the igus Robot Control (iRC) software — browser-based drag-and-drop programming — with a Python API, ROS driver and Modbus TCP/TCP-IP interfaces, and mounts on tables, mobile bases or gantries. It's not a high-accuracy industrial arm; its niche is accessible, lightweight automation for pick-and-place, inspection, lab work and light assembly where cost and simplicity matter more than sub-millimetre repeatability.

name: Meca500
desc: The Mecademic Meca500 is, by the maker's account, the smallest and most compact six-axis industrial robot arm — and one of the most precise, with ±0.005 mm repeatability (five microns) that few arms of any size match. Reach is 330 mm from the flange (260 mm from wrist) with a 500 g rated payload (1 kg maximum under conditions), from a 4.6 kg body with the controller built inside. Its design philosophy is what sets it apart: rather than a stand-alone system with a pendant and its own software suite, the Meca500 is a plug-and-work slave component that integrates into any PC or PLC over Ethernet with no training courses, installs or add-on purchases — controlled by simple TCP/IP ASCII commands, a Python API, a web interface, or industrial fieldbuses (EtherCAT, PROFINET, EtherNet/IP) on the relevant variants. Powered by the PS200 module (90–250 VAC), offered in R3 and R4 revisions, it's a staple of precision electronics, semiconductor, lab-automation and micro-manipulation cells where footprint and accuracy dominate.

name: xArm 6
desc: The UFACTORY xArm 6 is the arm that made 5 kg-class manipulation affordable for labs and startups — 5 kg payload across 700 mm reach at ±0.1 mm repeatability and 1 m/s top speed, at roughly half the price of mainstream 6-axis rivals, which has made it one of the most common arms in mobile-manipulation and embodied-AI research stacks. Its aluminium and carbon-fiber structure is driven by outer-rotor brushless motors through industrial harmonic drives with 17-bit multi-turn absolute encoders, drawing a typical 200 W through the AC control box and mounting in any orientation (IP40, cleanroom-suitable). The software story is its second superpower: UFACTORY Studio's full GUI with drag-and-drop and simulation, open-source Python and C++ SDKs over Ethernet, Blockly, and official xarm_ros/ros2 packages, with a native ecosystem of grippers, vacuum tools and camera mounts. Collision detection and control-box e-stop cover safety basics for supervised light-industrial and research use.

name: Lite 6
desc: The UFACTORY Lite 6 is a compact 6-axis tabletop arm built for benches where footprint and setup speed matter more than precision — 600 g payload across 440 mm reach at ±0.5 mm repeatability and 500 mm/s top speed, with the controller integrated so the whole system is arm-plus-Ethernet-cable. Its aluminium and carbon-fiber structure pairs direct-drive motors with harmonic drives to balance durability against cost (typical draw 150 W), and it inherits UFACTORY's full open software stack: Studio's drag-and-drop GUI, open-source Python and C++ SDKs, Blockly, and official ROS/ROS 2 support — which has made it a staple in university labs, imitation-learning rigs and light-automation pilots. UFACTORY itself notes the Lite 6 is not certified as a collaborative robot despite its safe desktop scale, an honest distinction most competitors skip. A Kit variant bundles the Lite Gripper and Lite Vacuum Gripper.

name: RO1
desc: The Standard Bots RO1 is an AI-native American-made cobot (built in Glen Cove, New York) that pairs class-leading hardware with GPT-level no-code programming — a best-in-class 18 kg payload across 1,300 mm reach at ±0.025 mm repeatability, positioned at roughly half the price of comparable arms with leasing from about $5/hour. Its arm uses six CAN-bus joints, each with two encoders, two independent torque-sensing methods and fail-safe brakes that engage on power loss — the basis of built-in collision detection and force limiting for fenceless work. Uniquely in its class it ships with an onboard 3D machine-vision system for object detection, screen reading and pick-without-programming, and can be programmed by natural language, a no-code touchscreen, or a Python API/SDK, learning new tasks from a single demonstration. It mounts without bolting into concrete for fast redeployment. Practical limits are documented openly: default tooltip speed 0.75 m/s, with speed reduced to 25% above 16 kg payload. Standard Bots (GE Appliances partner; $63M Series B) targets high-mix machine tending, inspection and palletizing up to 30 cases/min.

name: Gen3
desc: The Kinova Gen3 is one of the most widely used research manipulators in the world — an ultra-lightweight 7-axis arm (8.2 kg, 4 kg mid-workspace payload, 902 mm reach) chosen by hundreds of universities, startups and corporate labs for its portability and sub-30-minute setup. Its distinguishing features are research-grade: 1 kHz closed-loop low-level control, infinite-rotation joints, and Kinova smart actuators with integrated torque sensors plus current, voltage and temperature sensing for precise force control and rich state feedback. An optional Kinova Vision module integrates an Intel RealSense RGB-plus-depth camera directly at the end effector (30 cm–∞ colour, 18 cm–∞ depth) for perception work. It's driven through the Kortex API in C++ or Python with official ROS/ROS 2 kortex drivers, over Gigabit Ethernet from 24 VDC, and offered in 7-DoF, 6-DoF (891 mm) and Gen3 lite forms — the combination of light weight, torque sensing and open software making it a default arm for mobile-manipulation and imitation-learning research.

name: OB7
desc: The Productive Robotics OB7 is an American-made (Carpinteria, California) 7-axis collaborative robot whose defining features are its extra joint and its no-code philosophy. The seventh axis gives it human-like dexterity to reach around obstacles and work in confined spaces that 6-axis arms can't, at a 5 kg payload and 1,000 mm reach. Its bigger differentiator is programming: OB7 is taught by demonstration — 'show, don't program' — so operators physically guide it through tasks with no code, no scripting and minimal training, which Productive Robotics markets as the simplest cobot to deploy. An optional OB7 Vision system adds camera-based part detection. Certified for fenceless collaboration (ISO 10218-1 / ISO/TS 15066), it targets CNC machine tending, assembly, pick-and-place, packaging and finishing for small and mid-size manufacturers, and comes in a family including longer-reach Stretch and higher-payload Max8/Max12 variants. Built for fenceless palletizing and end-of-line packaging, it also handles harsh work — machine-tool loading, welding — thanks to IP67 sealing with a special drip-proof coating against coolants and dust, plus food-grade grease for food and pharma use. High-resolution torque sensors in each of its six joints enable fenceless human collaboration certified to PL d Cat. 3 with 25 distinct safety functions, including configurable envelopes, dual retract moves (Retract & Clamp-Release) and a Pushback function to move the arm aside during operation. Yaskawa targets easy entry: the tablet-based Smart Pendant guides programming and safety config with hand-guiding and Smart Frame, backed by Wizard programming, a plug-and-play accessory ecosystem, MotoSim offline simulation, and a choice of YRC1000 or compact YRC1000micro controllers.

name: MagicDog Y1
desc: MagicLab's industrial flagship quadruped: IP67 aviation-grade body carrying 45 kg dynamically (150 kg standing) at up to 6 m/s, climbing 60 cm obstacles, 25 cm stairs and 45° slopes, with 3D LiDAR + dual depth + dual optical perception, centimeter positioning, hot-swap batteries and modular payload expansion for inspection and logistics.
